utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. We will now resume the hearing. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is everybody here? The interpreter is here, good morning. Let's begin. Mr. Cayley, I think is going to be questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, learned counsel. The next witness is Captain Jean Marc Lanthier, a Canadian army officer who served from 1992 to 1994. If you wish, I'll move straight into the summary of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness served with the Canadian battalion, which was the Canadian government's contribution to the United Nations protection force in Bosnia-Herzegovina from October 1992 to May 1993 and then he completed a second tour from October 1993 until May of 1994. The Canadian battalion was based in the municipality of Visoko, which is a municipality which borders on the municipality of Kiseljak. The larger part of his testimony will be concerned with events that he witnessed in the municipality of Kiseljak. He will speak, first of all, to you about the HVO military command structure and will, in fact, relate to you two conversations which he had, one with Mr. Mario Bradara in the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak, about the structure of the HVO and its command elements, and then a subsequent conversation which he had with General Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic, in Vitez, who confirmed to him, the structure, as explained by Mr. Bradara and confirmed that all of the HVO forces in the Kiseljak command were under his own command, under Colonel Blaskic's command. He will speak to you of his experience in the Busovaca joint commission very briefly, as an observer, and he will relate to you his understanding of the relationship, as he saw it, between the then Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Dario Kordic. He will then speak of events after the 16th of April, in the municipalities of Vitez and Kiseljak. He will very briefly relate to you, what he saw of the village of Ahmici and the mosque in that village. He will speak of two attempted visits to Colonel Blaskic at the HVO headquarters in Vitez to try and get a better understanding of what was going on at the time. The two visits were unsuccessful. He will explain to you why that occurred. He will then relate to the court the violence and destruction which subsequently occurred in the municipality of Kiseljak and he will relate to the court his knowledge of the destruction which took place in a number of Bosnia Muslim villages, after the 16th of April. Particularly, he will relate to you his knowledge of the village of Rotilj, he will give to the court the detention of civilians, the inhuman treatment of those civilians, the use of able-bodied men for the digging of trenches. He will relate to you numerous complaints that he made about what he saw taking place to the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak. He will tell you of the explanations that were given to him by the headquarters in Kiseljak, as to the nature of the military operation that was taking place and the peculiar security practices of the HVO, in relation to Bosnian Muslim civilians. He will relate to you his knowledge of the detention of civilians, in the HVO headquarters at Kiseljak, in the barracks, and will explain to you that his questions in this area ultimately ended in death threats being made against him by the HVO. He will then briefly speak to you of his second tour in Bosnia from October 1993 to May 1994 and this will concern, particularly, events in the municipality of Fojnica. He will explain to you that during this time, the Canadian battalion took upon itself the running of two hospitals for the mentally and physically handicapped in the towns of Bakavici and Drin. He will explain that the Canadian battalion took on this responsibility because staff had fled as a result of combat activities. He will explain to you, how the HVO forbid any member of staff to return to the Bakavici hospital, how ultimately the hospital was used by the HVO for covering and concealment during combat operations and how the HVO utilised mental patients in order to clear mine fields, in the area. He will to speak to you of how HVO -- how UNPROFOR convoys were continually fired upon by the HVO on their journey between Kiseljak and Fojnica. And he will speak to you of one particular convoy of medical and essential supplies for these two hospitals which had been previously authorised by the HVO from Kiseljak and then was attacked, even though a symbol of the Red Cross was prominently displayed on the convoy. He will explain of the complaint he made to the HVO headquarters about the attack on the convoy. In the final part of his testimony, he will speak to you concerning the knowledge of his presence of organised units in the municipality of Kiseljak. He will speak to you of his understanding of the effectiveness of the chain of command of the HVO and the communication facilities available to the HVO, both in terms of electronic transmission through radio and facsimile and telephone links and through road links between the various areas under HVO control. Finally, he will give you his professional opinion, as a soldier, on the nature of the military operation that he saw taking place during his first tour of duty in the municipalities of Vitez and Kiseljak. The evidence is relevant, I believe, to paragraphs 3 and 4, 5, 5.1 and 5.2. It's relevant to count 1, the persecution charge, paragraph 6.0 to 6.7, counts 2 to 4, the unlawful attack charges, paragraph 8, counts 5 to 10, the wilful killing and serious injury charges. Paragraph 9, counts 11 to 13, destruction and plunder of property, paragraph 10 of the indictment, count 14, the destruction of institutions dedicated to religion, paragraph 11, and finally counts 15 to 20 which deals with the inhumane treatments and taking of civilians as hostages. That's paragraphs 12 to 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. That was very clear, Mr. Cayley. We will stick with that plan and I'll tell that to the witness so that we can -- so we can try not to take any unnecessary delays. Your questioning, about how long do you expect to be asking questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One and a half to two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can have Captain Lanthier, is it Lanthier or Lanthier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Lanthier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Lanthier, yes, I see. Lanthier. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, give us your name, your first name and your rank. Please remain standing. In a few moments for you to read your declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I declare solemnly that I will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain, you may be seated. You have been called in by the Prosecution as part of the trial at the International Criminal Tribunal of General Blaskic who is here in this courtroom. As the judges have asked then, the Prosecutor has given us a resume of your testimony. Therefore, we're going to ask you not to get lost into details, but to remain with the major features of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Lanthier, L-A-N-T-H-I-E-R, is that right? You will stick with the main points in your testimony. Of course, it's being understood, if some of the points have been omitted, in that case, the Prosecutor will ask you the relevant questions. Mr. Cayley, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Captain Lanthier, if you can remember, and I will do the same, to speak fairly slowly to allow the interpreters to clearly interpret what you're saying, that will help matters along. I think I'm correct in saying that you joined the Canadian Armed Forces from university in 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are a Cavalry Officer and you commissioned into the 12th Armed Regiment in Canada based in Val-Cartier in Canada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you've done a number of jobs in the army, including troop leader, squad run battle officer, I think you remember staff officer to General Canes for two years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are, I think, a graduate of the command and staff college at Kingston and you are currently the operations officer of your regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that between October of 1993 and May of 1993, you served with the second Royal Canadian Regiment in Visoko in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second -- I'm sorry. The interpreter cannot hear the witness very clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Am I right in saying that between October of 1992 and May of 1993, you served with the second Canadian regiment in Visoko in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The name was the second Royal Canadian Regiment Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the regiment was delayed in Lipik, in the Republic of Croatia, for three months, and you actually deployed to Visoko in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Initially, we were supposed to go to Banja Luka and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we were delayed and it was only in the summer that we went there. We went to Visoko in the middle of February then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court very briefly what the mission of the Canadian Battalion was in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR mission for the Canadian battalion was to provide support to the UNHCR. At that time, we were talking about convoy escorting. That was the major mission of the Canadian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown exhibit 329. I'll just inform the technical staff there's a scatter pattern on the television screen, but I think everybody has this exhibit in front of them, without wasting any more time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Lanthier, what does this map represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This represents principally the Canadian Battalion's area of responsibility in 1993 when we arrived. Perhaps I'll use the document because you don't see it very clearly on the screen, but this was the municipality in which the Canadian Battalion was based in Visoko. The other sectors in which we operated were the following: Visoko, Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, Vares, Olovo, Busovaca. We were not responsible for Busovaca, but we would go by it in order to get to Kiseljak, so I was very familiar with that sector. Sometimes we had a company that was deployed and there was also a platoon that was near Visaje, and we would use it in order to move about in the area. The sectors that are dark show the sectors where the Canadian battalion was responsible, and that was a sector that I was very familiar with because I worked in that sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position with the Canadian battalion from February to mid-May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the deputy to the officer. What I would do then in my sector I was responsible for, the three military parties were there. The Bosnian forces from the government, they were called the BiH forces. There was the HVO, and there was the Bosnian-Serb army, there were the three factions there, and we tried to establish liaisons among them to be sure that we could be free to move about in order to do our work and to be sure, also, that we would have the freedom of movement for the UNHCR in our sector of responsibility. At the same time, as part of the same responsibility, but this was not an implicit function, not an explicit one, I had to act as a liaison -- responsible for the liaison with the UNHCR with the field officers. This was the term that was used, "field officers," in order to work on site, and then my role was to determine to what extent humanitarian assistance was needed in our sector of responsibility. I would be in contact with the UNHCR as a person who was able to give to the UNHCR daily briefings about the status of the situation where the fighting was taking place, and the needs, if there were any needs for convoy escorting. That is a summary, more or less, of my responsibilities. Although I was the deputy for the officer for the military parties, we were not able to stay in contact with the Serbs there. We had daily contact with the BiH forces and with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Lanthier, if I could ask you to consciously slow your pace down, I suffer from the same thing, unfortunately, because then the interpreters will find it easier to interpret what you're saying. Just to summarise, the essence of your duty was to act as a liaison officer between the three belligerent parties, the Bosnia government forces, the Bosnian-Serb forces and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think, as liaison officer, shortly after you arrived in Theatre, you needed to establish contact with the local headquarters or commands of the three warring factions, and I wonder if you can tell the court about how you went about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived, we began to deploy in the middle of February. During the first week, we set up our camp in Visoko, so I didn't start working as a liaison immediately, even though in that sector where we had arrived was not under the responsibility of UNPROFOR, as such, but rather the British Battalion that was in Vitez at that point. There was, who had already established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is middle of February now? You arrived in the middle of February; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point, the British liaison officer had already established certain contacts with the various forces on the ground. He delegated these responsibilities to me because now he had to concentrate only on the British battalion sector. He quickly showed me the locations of the various headquarters in my area of responsibility, without really introducing me to the commanders, except for one of the brigades, the BiH brigade, the 365th, I believe it was. Mr. Sinad -- I don't remember his last name. Sinad was his first name, but I don't remember his last name. We were the new arrivals, if you like, and we had to go meet the various commanders of the different headquarters. The first headquarters where I went was the one that was in Kiseljak, in the Kiseljak barracks. The commander, when I arrived, introduced himself to me as Mr. Ivica Rajic. The first reaction of Mr. Rajic was that he was not particularly interested in discussing anything with me on that day, but that he would rather that I refer to his Mario Bradara and said that he, Mr. Bradara, was responsible for the discussions with me and that I should speak with him for any points that I wanted to talk about. I also knew somewhat of the organisation -- something of the organisation, the HVO in our area of responsibility. And also explained in very general terms The British officer had explained the sector to me and also explained how the forces were distributed on the ground. And when I spoke with Mr. Bradara, I asked him to explain to me how the -- what was the chain of command and what was the structure, the structure of the forces, that is, the HVO forces in our area of responsibility in Central Bosnia, because obviously the chain of command was not limited only to ours, our sector but overflowed into another one as well. It was therefore clear, as Mr. Rajic had said, I was explained the lower structures. There were four units. The four subordinate headquarters of Mr. Rajic were in the Municipality of Vares, Krosova, Kiseljak and Fojnica. That was the lower structures on the ground. As far as the size of the forces of Kiseljak, I really wasn't quite sure, were they brigades, were they battalions, I really didn't know. I wasn't told whether it was a brigade or a battalion, but I was told that there were four municipalities. The four units did answer to Kiseljak and that was the operational group which answered to a higher force which was commanded by General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The transcript has stopped. It's not coming up. --- Short pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, that it's not actually working at the moment, so there is no simultaneous transcript being produced. I'm being informed, Mr. President, would it be appropriate for us to take a break in order for them to sort out the technical problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: --- Proceedings reconvened at 10.40 a.m. 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. Please be seated. I think that we will take a break around 11:30. Let's go on. Perhaps we should go back a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. President, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 330.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Lanthier, remembering to speak perhaps deliberately slowly, if you could go back to your visit to the HVO barracks in Kiseljak and your meeting with Mr. Rajic and Mr. Bradara, where Mr. Bradara explained to you the command structure of the HVO in central Bosnia, and if you could refer to this diagram whilst you're explaining that. One question before you answer that main question, did you, in fact, draw this diagram out for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm the one who prepared this. When we met, I explained to you, because I was asked to make an organisational chart and that's what I did. When I met Mr. Bradara, I was told what this represents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could run through the area concerning Kiseljak and just briefly summarise to the court what Mr. Bradara led you to understand was the structure in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, it was explained to me during the meeting with Mr. Bradara that Kiseljak, that is, the headquarters, was responsible for four regions that you can see here at the bottom, Fojnice, Kresevo, Kiseljak, and Vares. These four units or formations, I didn't know how large they were, and it was later on when I went on site, I was able to see how large they were, specifically Vares. The Kiseljak was also a brigade. It was the Ana Esic brigade. Kresovo and Fojnice, I was never really sure whether they were battalions or brigades. The four missions or units were under the command of the operational group of the HVO in Kiseljak. Kiseljak answered to Vitez, which was a headquarters for the operational zone level for central Bosnia which was commanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just clarify a number of points with you, what was the name of the brigade in Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bobovac, I think it was called, the Bobovac brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bobovac brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kiseljak, what was the name of the brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ban Jelacic brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ban Jelacic brigade. Now, all of the structure in Kiseljak and this subordinate units, this was represented to you by deputy commander Mario Bradara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was during that discussion when I was asked for an explanation of the forces on the ground, I learned that the Vares sector was an enclave at that time because it was surrounded by the BiH and the Bosnia-Serb army on the right side. In Kiseljak, there were also forces. I asked them to explain to me the chain of command and the formations for all these units in my sector of responsibility, and it was at that point that he explained to me how things were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you subsequently paid a visit to Colonel Blaskic in Vitez because Mr. Bradara explained to you that Mr. Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic, was the superior commander based there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I decided to visit the Vitez headquarters of General Blaskic. Although Vitez was not in my sector of responsibility, the Vitez area was under the responsibility of the British battalion which was based in Vitez, but it was important for me to introduce myself to Colonel Blaskic, and the reasons which were behind this visit were the fact that we were new in the region. We were working on a part of the ground which was under the control of the HVO which was under the command and control of Colonel Blaskic. Therefore, for me, it was important to introduce myself and to introduce the Canadian battalion to General Blaskic at that time. It was also important for me to know, to meet Rajic's superior. Since I'm a military person, the chain of command is very crucial and I have to know if there is a problem in the Kiseljak or Vares area that I should be able to go up the chain of command in order to settle the problem on a higher level. This is why I made an appointment with Colonel Blaskic and after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go slowly. Please go slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had an appointment with Colonel Blaskic and that's when I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, did you ask Colonel Blaskic about the chain of command going from his headquarters to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing at that visit was to introduce myself and to introduce the Canadian Battalion as well, to describe its mission, and to explain how it worked. Then I explained why I had come to see him, and I explained that it was for the reasons that I just told you, and I also told him that it was important for me to know that if there were problems that I couldn't settle, I should be able to work with the Kiseljak area. He told me, in fact, that area was under his control, that is, in control of those forces -- of the area in which the Canadian forces were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did, in fact, Colonel Blaskic say to you that all HVO forces in the Kiseljak area were under his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, yes, he confirmed to me that the Kiseljak operational group headquarters answered directly to him and that he controlled and commanded it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You concluded from that that the subordinate units in Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak, and Vares all ultimately answered to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through the Kiseljak headquarters. That is, the chain of command as I understood it at that time, and General Blaskic explained to me that starting from the army headquarters, which was located in Mostar, because he answered to Mostar, and it controlled Kiseljak which, in turn, controlled the four units or formations that appear on the organisational chart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like him to repeat this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I had said, as it was explained to me and what I understood, is that Colonel Blaskic who commanded the Vitez operational zone and that he was under the command of the army general command which was in Mostar, and Vitez controlled the operational group which was located in the barracks in Kiseljak, and they were controlled by the Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak and Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I also right in saying that at that meeting, Colonel Blaskic said that, although his door was always open, it wouldn't be necessary for you to visit him because Kiseljak was directly under his military order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The discussion that I had with Colonel Blaskic was one which was very friendly, and he certainly did mention that his door was always open to me, that I was welcome, and that if I wanted to see him, I just had to make an appointment. But I, according to him, wouldn't really have to see him again because I could settle my problems by speaking directly to people in Kiseljak, and Kiseljak answered to him directly. So, therefore, at that point, it was clear that I should address myself to Kiseljak in order to settle any problems in my sector of responsibility, because Kiseljak was responsible for all the forces that were located in this zone, the Canadian Battalion area of responsibility, but that if I did have a problem, I should not hesitate to contact him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have now indicated on this structural diagram, two other operational groups. Now, you're aware that they existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they explained to me what the general structure in Bosnia was, that is, as it relates to the HVO forces. I don't remember the details, the specific names of the operational groups and the other operational areas. I was particularly interested in the ones that had to do with my area of responsibility because that was where we principally operated, but it's true that I did know that there were other operational groups that existed as well. I was very aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that these other operational groups were under the command of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, similarly to what I just said about Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us return to Mr. Bradara who introduced himself to you as the deputy commander in Kiseljak. If the witness could be shown exhibit 331? Now, you have viewed a video, which is exhibit 260, and this is a still from that video. Who is the man that is identified by the red circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Mario Bradara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown exhibit 332, again, this is a still from exhibit 260. Do you recognise the man there with the red circle around his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also Mr. Bradara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you meet Mario Bradara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my first tour in Bosnia, it would be hard for me to tell you exactly how many times now, but I met him several times a week. The first time I met him was around the end of February and I left in the middle of May, I guess, about 30 or 40 times. I couldn't tell you exactly, but many times and regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a fair enough approximation. Now, just to conclude on the meetings that you had with Mr. Bradara and Mr. Blaskic, when did they occur, those two meetings, an approximate time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably the first week of March in '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are the two meetings where the command structure of the HVO was explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bradara, can you tell the court how he was dressed when you met him, what types of uniform he wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Bradara stood out. Well, the only two times I saw him in uniforms, once he was wearing a black uniform, one with two badges, one of the HVO forces in Bosnia and the second, I really don't remember what it represented. The only other uniform I ever saw him wear was an urban camouflage uniform. It was a grey/white uniform which one would usually use when fighting in urban areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mario Bradara always able to make decisions on his own or did you observe him referring up the chain of command to give you decisions about various matters involving the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impression that I received is that on several occasions, the only thing I could actually get from Mr. Bradara would be given later. I would get the answers to questions that I would ask later on. Even though he had been delegated authority by Mr. Rajic during the first meeting that I had with them, Mr. Bradara would regularly consult him for important decisions, that is, consult his superior, when I say "him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're referring to his superior, you mean Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you gained the impression while you were there that the chain of command was actually working, that subordinates were referring to superiors and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move on now in time and I would like you to explain to the court your recollection of your attendance at the Busovaca joint commission. I think that happened in the first week of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. In early March, the first or second week of March 1993, I was not an active member of the Busovaca commission. However, I was invited by one of the members of the ECMM who was, himself, a member, and I attended then just as an observer, rather than as an actual member. My role was not as an active participant, but rather as a listener. I went to follow the discussions that were taking place in the context of that joint Busovaca commission about activities in the field, which I was familiar with, at least with regard to the military and the humanitarian activities within the area of responsibility of -- it was in that capacity that I was invited. I was participating in an inactive way in this joint Busovaca commission. The first meeting I attended, there were several people attending there. Of course, there were representatives of the ECMM. There were also the military observers and there were also various representatives from various factions. There was Flarjo Nakic who was in charge of the operational zone of Vitez and there were also members of the third core in Mirodan. And also a another person whose name escapes me now, but these were the people who attended the first meeting I attended. I did not attend a large number of such meetings. Under the umbrella of this same commission, in the spirit of this commission, I attended as an observer other meetings which, I believe, were referred to as coordination commissions. These, particularly, the various deputy commanders -- rather, did not join the different deputy commanders, but rather the commanders of the different factions, and on two or three occasions, I attended in which Colonel Blaskic was present and Mr. Stuart was the commander of the British Battalion in Vitez. There was also the commander of the third core. There was also Dario Kordic and also a woman from the political wing, from Bosniak, and I don't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to the court the interaction that you saw taking place between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, I was there as an observer, and so I was not at the table as an active participant, but rather sitting further back, and so I participated in a meeting with one of the translators who was helping me and I was introduced to. During the first meeting, I spoke with Mr. Dario Kordic, who was introduced to me as one of the head political persons for the Bosnians in Croatia. When I heard the conversations and the discussions that took place, my impression was that Kordic could be described as an advisor in political matters to Colonel Blaskic. This is, at least, the impression I had and that I was able to understand from the discussions that took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the transcript, you stated that he was one of the head political persons for the Bosnians in Croatia. I think you probably mean the other way around. Was he one of the head political persons for the Bosnian Croats in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe from what you saw and from what your interpreter was telling you of the relationship between the then Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regards to the military issues, because, as far as I remember, this meeting covered a large number of issues, economic questions, also military and also social and humanitarian issues. What I was able to note and what interested me, in particular, was the military issues, particularly dealing with the warring factions. My perception was that, as I stated earlier, Mr. Kordic was a political advisor, but as far as military events were concerned, it was Colonel Blaskic who, indeed, had the last word and took decisions or gave his agreement to any type of activity taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think on the 17th of April, you visited a Bosnian army, Bosnian government force commander, at the operational group based at Istok, and I think he told you about his concerns in the municipality of Vitez, and I wonder if you could tell the court about that meeting and then about your subsequent visit to the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe to clarify, first of all, why I was meeting with the commander of Istok based at Visoko, which was the camp based at Visoko, which is 300 or 400 metres from the headquarters of the operational group of Istok. This was a Muslim operational group which was patrolling the various Muslim brigades in our area of responsibility. Now, this headquarters covered the 302nd brigade and also the 304th brigade, which is located in Brezja. These were close to our camp. Therefore, the relations I had with this headquarters, I had the intentions of beginning my day with the meetings with the Istok headquarters and also meeting with Memisevic where I would receive reports on the situations and things that had occurred during the recent time. This would enable me to find out what was going on in my area of responsibility, which, perhaps, I myself was not able to observe. And this was how I was able to obtain information about what was going on. Later on, I would be able to look in more detail to what was going on. So these daily meetings, as I said, took place with Mr. Memisevic in which he would indicate to me that in the Vitez pocket there seemed to be a conflict taking place and that the Muslim civilians living in the Kiseljak pocket were victims of an attack that had been launched by the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt. You just said the Bosnian Muslim civilians living in the Kiseljak pocket were the victims of attack, I think you were being told at this time about Muslim civilians living in the Vitez pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed. These were Muslim civilians in the Vitez pocket that were victims of an attack and, at that time, there were several houses that were burned and there were some civilians who were being taken prisoner and there were some crimes committed against them. He asked me whether or not I was in a position to give him any information about the report that he had received. At that point, I had no information that would enable me to confirm or deny the information in that report. And so I decided myself to go to the Vitez pocket, although Vitez itself was not within my area of responsibility. My feeling was that if something were to occur in the Vitez pocket, which is the impression that Mr. Memisevic had, that these same attackers could perhaps actually spread to attack the Kiseljak pocket area. So my first reaction, therefore, was to go to the Vitez area to see and decide whether or not, indeed, something was going on and also to meet with Colonel Blaskic to obtain more details about what, indeed, occurred. So I took the road and I went through Vitez pocket to go to the headquarters located in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What day was that, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the 18th or the 19th, I believe, of April. So going through the Vitez pocket, which I would go through on a regular basis, because I had to regularly visit the British battalion in Vitez, I noted that there was, indeed, some residences or buildings that had been burned and there, indeed, had been fighting in the city. The city itself, the city of Vitez, was much more quiet than normally, and it gave me the impression that it was a ghost town, and that is one way that I can describe the feeling I had when I arrived there. When I arrived at the Vitez headquarters, with the intention of meeting with Colonel Blaskic, outside the hotel itself, outside the entrance to the hotel were the headquarters, I was told there was no one available to meet with me. At that moment, I decided I should simply return and I returned to the Canadian camp. But while going along the main road, I passed by the Ahmici village to see even more what was going on. I noted that there were several residences that had been burned or destroyed and also that a Mosque, which had now been completely destroyed. My impression was that there had indeed been an attack, that had taken place, against the Muslim population in the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you, in fact, returned again at this time to the HVO headquarters in Vitez on a second occasion to try and see Colonel Blaskic about what saw had taken place in the municipality of Vitez. Can you tell the court about that second visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I still had not received a response. I had spoken with several offers of the Britbat who had given me some details, so I was in a position to note something had occurred in the Vitez pocket, but I needed more information given the fact that we normally -- in the cases of conflicts, whether we need more information to see whether this could spread to the Kiseljak pocket. So I went to Vitez, once again, to meet with Mr. Blaskic, but on that occasion, I was able to go inside the headquarters, but I was not able to meet with Colonel Blaskic who was still absent. Mr. Rajic was not present either, but I was able to meet with one of his representatives who gave me some information and told me at that moment, that the deputy commander was not available, but he stated he -- whether he, as one of the other Staff Officers could give me some information or details about the activities that took place the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Transcript, the transcript indicates that Mr. Rajic was not present in the headquarters and I think in fact, you meant Mr. Nakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's what I said, Mr. Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position in the headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I interrupted you, you were just explaining that one of Colonel Blaskic's representatives, one of the staff offices in his headquarters met you. What did he say, to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The officer, not the representative of the staff of the headquarters, indicated that neither the commander, nor the deputy commanders were available. When I asked for some clarifications about the events which took place, the preceding days, he answered that he had no comment he could make on that issue and that that ended our discussion there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you returned to Visoko and you briefed your commanding officer about what you had seen in the Vitez municipality. Now, I would like to move to the 19th of April when I think you met with Mr. Memisevic again, and he told you this time of certain HVO activities that had commenced in the Kiseljak municipality. Can you tell the court about that occasion and what you subsequently did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The next day, the next morning on the 19th, I, again, met, as I did every morning, with Mr. Memisevic. At that time, he told me that he had received a report and informed me about the report, about the events that had taken place in Vitez on the day of the 16th and that the same events that were now occurring in the Kiseljak municipality, and he said that it seemed -- because he was not in a position to confirm in a very precise manner the details of that report, but he said that there were attacks against the Muslim citizens in the Kiseljak pocket, and he named a few villages which had a very large percentage of Muslim citizens. With this information, I decided to go through the Kiseljak pocket in order to confirm by site or on site whether or not such activities had taken place. So I went to the direct road, the long road, rather, through Busovaca going down the south-east to the Kiseljak pocket and at that moment, I did note that there were a number of or many houses that had been damaged and had been slightly burned and had been plundered and destroyed. Getting even closer to the city of Kiseljak, I noted in the northern part of the road, on a hill somewhere nearby, I noted that there was a heavy machine-gun that was firing into the houses from its position. It was a very constant machine-gun fire and here I had the impression that either -- from the fact that some of these houses were burnt, I had the impression that either there was some sort of flame that was used to ignite these houses or, perhaps, some sort of igniting shells that had been used to destroy these homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any fire being returned from these houses into which this heavy machine-gun was firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. All I could note was that it was a heavy fire coming from only one direction and it was not a battle, but rather an attack without any response. There was nothing at all that gave me the impression that this was a combat between two parties, but simply an attack on these residences. It would not indicate to me that they were of any military nature or putting up any defence involving combat, at least that's what I deduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also stated that you noted the houses appeared to become -- appear to be set on fire when these rounds of ammunition from this heavy machine gun hit them. Did you conclude what type of ammunition was being used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was that these were either incendiary bombs or some sort of tracer, something that's used to aid a cannon to follow the trajectory of a shell. If these tracers were to hit something that was flammable, then the objects would catch fire or perhaps they would also use an incendiary type of ammunition, and it would have the same effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you then visited the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak to try and discover what was taking place. Can you tell the court about that visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of my visit in going through the long path to Kiseljak was to get to Kiseljak. I could not go there directly without having some idea of what was going on. The main purpose of my visit was to see what the goings on were, and so I went to the Kiseljak barracks with the purpose of meeting with Mario Bradara. When I went to the barracks, I was told, quite simply, that at the main entrance to the Kiseljak barracks, there is a metal barrier that had been erected there, and I was told that Mr. Bradara was not available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you then briefed the United Nations protection forces in Kiseljak about what had taken place, and then you tried to gain access to the village of Rotilj. Can you please tell the court about your first attempt to enter that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I stated, when I left the headquarters of Kiseljak, the headquarters were UNPROFOR’s located quite close to the area of Kiseljak and so I stopped and I made a report to the head of the operations headquarters at UNPROFOR and also to the G-5 in dealing with civilians and military and at that moment, I went or rather I tried to go to the village of Rotilj. The reason I tried to go to this village was also -- is because this is one of the villages in which Mr. Memisevic had indicated, there was a large percentage of Muslims. When I approached -- when you try to go to the Kiseljak to this village, you have to take a secondary road on the left but I noted there was a road blocked that was being manned by some soldiers and also a police car, some Croatian soldiers. I was not able, therefore, to go all the way to the Rotilj village, because they prevented me from doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police and the soldiers at the roadblock, these were HVO soldiers and civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were civilian police. They were wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also HVO soldiers present at that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There were two or three soldiers. I don't know the exact number, but there were a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify matters, it's not particularly important, but you mentioned G-5. Am I right in saying that G-5 is a NATO term for a staff division that deals with civilian affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It is one of the branches of the headquarters, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you then returned to the battalion in Visoko and you briefed the commanding officer and the operations officer on what you had seen in the Kiseljak municipality. Then on the 20th of April, you, in fact, received permission to visit Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. On the 20th, I received authorisation to go to the Rotilj village with an escort. I was given two soldiers, two Croatian soldiers from the Kiseljak --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you, captain Lanthier, if the witness can be shown exhibit 333 because I think this will help you explain to the court. You say you received permission. From whom did you have to receive permission to enter Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the Kiseljak headquarters in order to obtain access, since there are two Croatian soldiers who had refused me access, to the Rotilj village. So I went to the headquarters in order to obtain authorisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're referring to the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you refer to Croatian soldiers, please specify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO, says the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could -- using the aerial photograph that is on the ELMO in front of you, if you could explain to the court your visit to Borina and Rotilj and what you discovered in those villages on the 20th of April, and if you could remember to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was given access to Rotilj with an escort, as I stated earlier. Now, the escort which preceded us, took one of the smaller roads which went to the west of Kiseljak and they introduced to us -- helped us get into Rotilj village. We were accompanied by a Mr. Colonel Landry, who was in this area, and also we were accompanied by a translator, so we went to Borina village which is identified here by circle 1 and they were told here this is Rotilj village. I don't know if this was an error in reading the map by our escort, and it was obvious at that point at least to Colonel Landry that this was not Rotilj village. We asked for permission of this escort, in order to leave from our vehicles, to get out of our vehicles and investigate a little closer some of the surroundings. They allowed us to do so and Colonel Landry and myself and also the translator walked on foot without an escort. At that moment, we went down the direction which is indicated by the arrow to the circle 2 where we went from Borina village to Rotilj village. When we went to Rotilj, we were welcomed by some 30 persons. Everyone was moving about in order to see us. It was the first UN presence that they had seen, since the events that had occurred just two days earlier. At that moment, they told us that there had been an attack that had taken place against Rotilj village and that there had been several crimes that had been committed. One of the first persons later on that came to present themselves to us directly, both to myself and Mr. Colonel Landry was about 30 years old or so and was living within the house. He came out of his house and came to us. And the man explained to us, that when the attack occurred, he had been outside of the house in his field since he was a farmer and that his wife who was alone in the house had been a victim of the rape and that all of the soldiers that had come into the house had raped her and then had been executed, that is she had been shot in the head. Even though the body was not there anymore, there was evidence to show that there had been a body there. The table and the lamp had dried blood on it, as well as the floor. There were several shells that were in the living room and several pieces of bone which had scattered and splattered at the bottom of the wall. So I was able to see the physical evidence of the -- I could see the physical evidence of the crime, even though I did not see the body and that was proof that there had been a crime committed there. Then we went out. There were other relatives there, other family -- relatives of the victim, family members, who introduced themselves to me and to Colonel Landry and we had been told that there had been -- the house next to it had been killed, there was a 40-year-old man and a young teenager who had been caught on the main road, and they were executed and after that, their heads had been cut off. Where I was taken, the bodies weren't there any more, but you could still see pools of blood and pieces of brain that were lying on the ground. There was a woman there that told me that her husband had been captured and he had been burned with car battery acid and then I couldn't see whether this person had been executed by the bullets, but he was a victim, in any case. I didn't see the remains, but that was at the cemetery near the entrance to the village and we were shown where the bodies were buried in the cemetery. There were eight locations where you could see that the earth had been moved and that the earth was still moist and then I was told -- I do remember that I was told there were 17 people who were victims of the attack. From what I understood, the members of the same family had been buried in a common grave, and that's why there were fewer graves than victims. When I asked a few questions, because I wanted further explanation, I wanted to know how the attack occurred, and I was explained that on the evening of the 18th, there were soldiers who had appeared who had taken control of the perimeter of the city so that nobody could get out and that in the middle of the village, a heavy machine gun had been set up and there were soldiers who went from house to house, pulling the people out, and then at that point, there was communication which -- so that I had the impression that it was a command post that was on the ground, somewhat north of Rotilj, and that there had been a communication with them and then they went from house to house and some of the houses, some of the people had been executed. So the impression that I immediately had was that it was an attack which had been carried out according to infantry platoon tactics which you will find in urban combat in defence of the perimeter, communications, that was a term that we use, fighting in built up areas, and that's the impression that we had. So Colonel Landry and I continued to walk. You can see there's a third circle, number 3, and we went there to see what had happened. There were several houses, especially in what's covered by circle number 2, the houses that were burned. Then we went to the east and there was less destruction there. That's what happened during my first visit to the village of Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can conclude my questions after the break, Mr. President, on this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Witness enters court room).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we're now going to resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the ELMO could be illuminated, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain Lanthier, we were talking about the aftermath of an attack that you witnessed in the village of Rotilj. Did the villagers identify the soldiers who attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correction about the question, I was not present at the attack. I got information from the survivors -- the victims who told me what they had seen. I was not an eye witness to any of it, but what I was told is -- the term that they used was they were HVO soldiers who had committed the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a number of houses had been burned down, and I wonder if you can indicate on the photograph where you saw houses that were burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mainly in this -- what's in the circle No. 2. I can't tell you individual houses. This is some time later now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in area 3, did you notice any houses that were burned in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I remember that there was some, but the level of discussion (sic) wasn't nearly anywhere what I indicated in the circle marked 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the transcript indicates that the 'level of discussion' wasn't nearly anywhere what I indicated in circle marked 2. I think you meant the level of destruction was not anywhere near that which you had seen in circle No. 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is happening with the transcript. It seems that this is frequent, we're having a lot of basic and frequent errors with the transcript. Can you explain this to us, Mr. Registrar. Not only the names, but there's meaning which is changed too. I'm not blaming anybody for this, but we have to be concerned about it. We can't use a transcript which has errors. Mr. Cayley is being very careful about the transcript, but it can't be easy to ask questions and then to make sure that the sense of the question has been indicated properly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, this is a new team and we will look into the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's a new team. There are really mistakes, serious errors. It's worrisome. Beyond the technical questions itself, I'm asking the team who is working there with all the understanding of the difficulties of doing the transcript, but to be careful. Perhaps the witness could speak a little bit more quietly. If you like, we could change the team. We have new teams that come in to work. We have a new courtroom. But I would like the transcript to be correct and reflect what the transcript has said because when the cross-examination comes, the Defence is going to use the transcript. All right. That's all I have to say. Speak slowly, let's try to work in such a way that errors are limited as much as possible. Thank you very much. Proceed. THE WITNESS; To answer your question, the level of destruction which I remember seeing in circle 3 was much less than what you see in No. 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Captain Lanthier, how did you and the individuals who accompanied you react to what you saw in the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My initial reaction was horror, horror, horror, in the face of the savagery of the acts, in the violence. The aggressiveness that was demonstrated by the attack, which I didn't see, but of which the physical evidence was still there, and it was really absolutely stunning, it was a reaction of disgust, both on my part and Colonel Landry, because Colonel Landry was speaking about one of the victims, or speaking with one of the survivors of the victims -- of the family of the victims was really - burst into tears when she told what had happened. The very human nature of these acts was just horrifying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on, and if the witness could be shown Exhibit 334. One final point, Captain Lanthier. Why do you believe that the HVO, first of all, took you to the village of Borina rather than to the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was that it was deliberate, they didn't want us to find out what had happened. That's the impression I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the village of Borina was in tact; was it not. How far was the village of Rotilj from the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A. If you look at it on a line along the road - well, on average we talk about 1,500 to 2,000 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you in fact before you could answer one of my questions. The village of Borina, was that in tact when you visited, the first village that you visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were in Borina, I don't remember having seen any destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have Exhibit 334 in front of you and I wonder if you can tell the court about the visits that you made on either the 21st or the 22nd of April of 1993 to those villages and if you could recall for the court what you saw in those villages that are highlighted on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went Bakovici to the villages that you see in orange. During my first visit, we were going along the main road but I couldn't get into the villages themselves. As I said, there was firing directed at some of the houses. And as a liaison officer, the only thing I had was a jeep with a vinyl roof, so I didn't have any armoured protection which would allow me to go into the sector where the firing was going on and which was still heavy. But several days later when it seemed that the attack was over, I went to the villages and I got out of my vehicle and I walked about within the village in order to try to understand exactly whether or not there was any kind of evidence about what had happened. And I went into several houses myself. The first thing I saw when I went in is that I didn't have to break the door open because the doors had either been torn off or were just torn open. I would go into the houses, I could see that there had been theft, there had been vandalism which makes me think that the contents of the drawers had been thrown out on the floor. There was broken glass on the floor and all of this showed me that there had been vandalism within the house. The houses had also been burned, some of the houses that were next to the barns. There was dead cattle and others, there was still cattle but it was in very, very bad condition, and we could see that it had deliberately been sacked. And for the purposes of the transcript those are the villages of Svinjarevo, Gormionica, Gromiljak, Polje Visjnica and Visjnica. I think you had earlier, as you already explained to the court, made a journey to Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These were the villages which are indicated in orange on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think in a stretch of road past the village of Gromiljak you came across house that was undamaged, and I wonder if you can tell the court about that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was going from village to village, something which particularly struck me, was just on the northern part of the road there was a group of three isolated houses, two of which on the ends were destroyed, but the one in the middle was absolutely in tact, one could see there was activity in the house. I went to the house, the one in the middle that was in tact and I asked to speak to the people who lived there. The person who was in the house at that point didn't want to answer me, didn't want to answer the questions he opened the door, but didn't want to speak to me. I then learned when I spoke with other people later on that the house belonged to a citizen of Croatian origin which, therefore, seemed to confirm to me that it was not - what had happened in the Kiseljak pocket is what is known as ethnic cleansing, where deliberately the citizens had been attacked, that is, those citizens of Muslim origin and only them. The others had been left untouched. It wasn't specifically the villages that were attacked, but specifically people within the villages. That was what allowed me - that is the conclusion I came to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any inhabitants in these villages when you visited them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The villages were deserted. The only thing that was left was some livestock, cows, chickens, but except for the house I mentioned to you around Gromiljak, I didn't see any presence of human beings in those villages. I don't know where their residents were at that point, and at that point I wasn't able to find any of the victims or any dead people lying in the houses. And I so I suppose that either they escaped during the attack and fled, or that they had been captured and, in that case, I was not in a position to determine what might have happened with the residents of those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think after seeing everything in the villages that are marked on this map you made a visit to the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak to see Mr. Mario Bradara. Can you tell the court about that visit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With what I was able to learn about the situation, it was clear that there had been ethnic cleansing, similar to what had been reported by the BRITBAT in the Vitez pocket. I went to the Kiseljak headquarters of the HVO in order to learn about what had happened, to get explanations about the events which had occurred. I met Mr. Bradara and his explanations at that time were that they were isolated acts which had been committed by citizens who revolted - who were sick of the situation and it was out of his control, something which happened just like that. He answered the same thing for the village of Rotilj, where he said there also they were isolated acts of citizens who revolted and frustrated, he used the word frustrated. My personal opinion, which I expressed to him at that time, is that I didn't believe that this was the result of simple - ordinary citizens but rather that these were synchronised acts, they had a military character. The very nature of the attack caused one to think of tactics that would be used in an infantry platoon in order to carry out something like this in the defence of a perimeter or defence of terrain or for communications. These were all indications that they were military activities, the fact that these took place in the Kiseljak pocket took place about 48 hours after what had happened in the Vitez pocket and that seemed to confirm to me that this was something which had been synchronised, it was not the result of chance. And then I explained my feelings to Mr. Bradara at that point and he answered, no, that's not the case at all, it's simply that these citizens got very excited and that's how they reacted to the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Bradara was lying to you about what had occurred in the Kiseljak pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was absolutely the impression that I had, that he was not being honest with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think subsequently you decided to make weekly visits to the village of Rotilj and I'd like you to explain to the court what occurred on those visits, and from whom you needed authority to visit the village of Rotilj in all of your visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I knew that Rotilj had actually been attacked and that it was the only place where I had still seen that there were people living after the attack. As I said, in the other villages all were abandoned, but Rotilj still had people living in it. And at that time I asked Mr. Bradara for authorisation to visit the village regularly which was granted to me and it was written in - it was going to be in writing 24 hours in advance saying that I could go once a week to the village of Rotilj for humanitarian purposes. The purpose of my visit was to be sure that the basic living conditions of those people would be sufficient and, therefore, I spoke about water and medicine, clothing, that is the basic commodities. When authorisation was given to me the first time and when I arrived in the village of Rotilj, as far as I remember there was a couple -- there was a couple there, or several hundred people there, I don't have the exact number of people who were there, but those were the people who were in detention in the village of Rotilj. Why do I say that they were in detention, I do say because I myself saw with my own eyes that they had been mainly women, children and especially old couples. In the village there was absolutely no men who could have been of fighting age, the people there were either very young, children or old people who would no longer be able to do very much at all. In advance I received authorisation from Bradara, I went to the village, I spoke to the people there and I was told that they were living in overcrowded conditions. They talked about -- they said there were sometimes more than 10 people living in one house. Drinking water was a problem even though there was an aquaduct and a well but the water available was not sufficient for the number of people in the village and there was also several health problems, and afterwards I often took representatives of the World Health Organisation with me, that is physicians, specialists, who could take care of people who are in a precarious condition. And then I was told - one could feel in the village, feel that they were detained, there were people - nobody was in handcuffs, nobody was being threatened by a weapon in front of me, but one had the feeling in this village, it was said, sort of, indirectly that nobody could try or would try to escape from that village. I don't have the document with me, when you look at the aerial photograph you can see that it's rather isolated, sort of in the fields, and it would be possible to escape during night. But what I gathered from speaking to the village residents is that nobody dared to try to escape because they were afraid if they were to flee there would be reciprocal measures against those who didn't escape. There was old people there, young children, very young people, and it would have been impossible for most of the people to - to make a mass escape. And then they were afraid. I certainly had the feeling that had they tried to escape there would have been something taken - gone against - there was old couple, when I say old couple I say they were about 60 years old and they explained to me that in April, 1992 they came to visit their family in Rotilj and that when he came - when they were about to go back to Sarajevo because they came from Sarajevo they were prevented from leaving Kiseljak and they were brought to Rotilj and, therefore, that couple was being held against their will. And this is since April of '92 and now this is April,' 93 and it was already a year that the couple was there. And they gave me the number of their son living in France so I could try to contact. I never was able to do so. But this is an example of people who were being held against their will. I had asked where the men were because you could see, as I said, that there were no men of fighting age in Rotilj, and I was then told that the men had been taken in the morning and they had been taken to the confrontation lines and that they were digging trenches during the day. This is the information that was given to me by the residents of the village. And with that information I went to see Bradara. After my first visit to the village of Rotilj, I asked him questions about what I had been told. I wanted to know why these people were being kept against their will. And Bradara said to me - answered me that it was for their own safety. That it was in order to avoid having what happened elsewhere happen to them and so it was for their own good they were being kept. When I asked why men were being taken to dig trenches, Bradara answered that they were not being forced to go, but they were volunteers, they were sympathisers of our cause, they were going of their own will to dig the trenches. That comment seemed absolutely ludicrous to me and I must - I said I couldn't believe that. I said that their relatives, their friends had been massacred and now he was telling me that they were going to dig trenches of their own will. It's hard for me to believe that. And I also suggested to Bradara that through the International Red Cross Committee there be organisations -- be organised help for them. Bradara, however, didn't want to accede to my proposal to get people help from the outside and all that he had said were two things, that in fact they were prisoners, they were detained against their own will and that, in addition to that, some of those residents or detainees were being used as forced labour on the front line. That's what my visits allowed me to conclude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm right in saying that the HVO readily admitted that they were using able-bodied men from Rotilj to dig trenches on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, please don't repeat things too often, we understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now just to describe the atmosphere in Rotilj, to make it absolutely clear what the atmosphere was like in this camp, could you explain to the Judges what you sensed the feelings of these people were in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not said openly. I was not under escort, but you can still feel the fear and almost a panic feeling among the people who were there. It seemed that they were trying to speak, but were not seeing -- or showing anyone that was visiting that they were actually speaking to me. Perhaps they felt like the walls had ears and that perhaps certain events would be told and they would be heard. So there was A palatable fear that was existing in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many times you complained about what was taking place in Rotilj to the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had visited the Rotilj village on a weekly basis, I would visit them three or four times the Rotilj village, from my first visit to the time of my departure and each time there would be someone who could come to see me, a detainee who would then tell me something, and then they would also beg us to try to intervene. Each time I sent my reports of these complaints to Mr. Mario Bradara, so three or four times after my visit and several other occasions. I was called in the course of my duties to see Mr. Bradara on several occasions, as I said, each week as well, but at least on four different occasions I mentioned and I made complaints to Mr. Bradara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Now, at the end of April and the beginning of May you had a report of civilian detainees in the Kiseljak barracks, and I'm going to place Exhibit 335 in front of you and with the use of that Exhibit I wonder if you can relate to the court your knowledge of the presence of civilian prisoners in the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that in the Kiseljak barracks there was some prisoners being held. At that time I had no proof that could confirm or deny what was being told to me about the Kiseljak - told to me in the Kiseljak village, rather. But in the barracks, during my regular visit with Mr. Bradara, I noted there were several children that were playing in the field right near the barracks, and it's surrounded by -- rather, the barracks that are indicated in circle No. 2, here you found the offices for the Kiseljak headquarters. And so in order to go to this location I had a very clear view of the barracks circled in No. 2 and I could see children playing there and I could also see some clothes drying on a line. There were some scarves and dresses and other clothing, and I cannot understand why these children or this clothing would be there. This is military barracks, it was not a sort of shelter, and so I wondered what was going on. And I asked Mr. Bradara who was detained, whether or not there was someone being detained in these barracks, and Mr. Bradara admitted that indeed there was 100 persons being detained in these barracks. When I asked why they were being detained, he responded that they were here for their own good in order to avoid that they be victims of attacks by other citizens in the Kiseljak pocket. I continued to question him and his answer was, well, if we were to free them then they would pose a threat to the HVO. A threat from women and children. That was something that -- what he was indicating to me. I didn't see where the threat was. And during subsequent visits, I requested permission to visit once again with these detainees to find out what conditions they were living because it seemed - to make sure they were adequate conditions living conditions but this authorisation was not given, I was not able to physically go there and visit with them. And during a meeting with Mr. Bradara I dropped this particular issue and I went on to other points on the agenda. Later on I went to visit in building No. 1. In order to get there you had to go through barracks in circle No. 2. So instead of going directly to this particular area I went - I kind of took a side road towards the barracks. I said I would go there quite frequently to the Kiseljak barracks, and to such a point that at the main gate when they see that I was the person in the vehicle they would let me come in even without asking for my UNPROFOR card or without identifying my identity because they knew me by sight. So they let me go all the way up to headquarters. Instead of going directly to the destination I attempted to go and visit with two buildings there circled in No. 2, but as I approached there was a guard that immediately intercepted me and redirected me into the proper direction towards headquarters. And when I entered into the Mr. Bradara's obvious, his office is what you get to when you turn to the right, second or third door to the right and so the window looks into the interior of the complex. And one of the first remarks he made to me was that I should have stopped asked questions - that I should not have stopped and asked questions, I should have let the subject drop. At the moment there was a solder there armed with a weapon who was pointing the weapon at me.
