So the clear message was - the message in that case, rather, was clear and I said I'm no longer going to bring there issue up and simply drop that discussion at that moment. When I was - I don't know what happened to those detainees then because I had to leave that location and after that I returned to Canada. So these were the circumstances in which I became aware of the presence of detainees in the Kiseljak barracks which presence was admitted by Mr. Bradara himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the photograph, the area circled 1 is the HVO headquarters building; is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's the building in which I had my meetings with Mr. Bradara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the arrow in circle 2 in one of those buildings, you recall that is where the civilian detainees were being kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't exactly remember whether it was the one more to the left or more to the right. It was in one of the two. That's why when they showed me the photo I circled both of them because I can't recall which one it was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the state of supplies into the Kiseljak pocket when you were there during your first tour, and when I talk about supplies I mean ammunition, food, fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One thing that was interesting that I noted right away after I arrived in central Bosnia was that the Kiseljak pocket and the small pocket in the northern area of my area of responsibility was that it was well supplied. What I mean by that is that the stores were open, things like chocolate, beer were available. There was no lack of fuel. And even the gas stations were open. Everything seemed to be working in a normal state. When I say that I mean that it did not seem to be an isolated pocket in the situation of war. I'd go to Visoko and elsewhere and all these kind of supplies did not exist in those areas, in areas controlled by Bosnian forces. In those cases these things were not available. So I was quite surprised to find the quality of life which was available in Kiseljak. When I talk about Kiseljak and environs. When I talk about Kiseljak, I am not talking about the city itself but the particular pocket, the enclave. And so all these supplies were available and I was quite surprised. Now I can give you an example of the prices. I can't remember the exact price for diesel, but I think it was a few Dutch marks in Kiseljak, three or four, but the same litre in Visoko you can obtain for some 20 Dutch marks and you can only obtain on the black market there, in Kiseljak you can obtain them in a regular gas station. I just on a curious note asked some people about there and I was told that, with some degree of pride I must add, that Croatia was in with convoys with resupplies, with fuel, diesel and all the things would come from Croatia would send - then be sent with convoys controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. And then to go through Kiseljak pocket because the Kiseljak pocket was in direct line with the Bosnian Serb army, so the way in which they would pay for this passage through there territory was with fuel, with diesel and gasoline or petrol. The biggest problem was getting fuel because there are sanctions that existed that prevented access to fuel. So there was definitely an agreement between the two parties, and Croatia would be able to meet the needs in Kiseljak. And I'm not sure what type of agreement existed but it was easy to see that such agreement did exist. I can also note that some of the munitions came from Croatia. What was told me - what led me to believe that was there were many types of munitions and you can also see different artillery cannons which are on a trailer which were being brought around the city and I could see those type of cannons, and there gave me there impression. And when I would come from Sarajevo to Kiseljak the road was blocked, and when I walked about one kilometre to go to where the block was, I can't remember the term in French, but there was MRS, it was a rocket launcher that was located there and this is a weapon that is not easy to make, and the fact that it was being used and that this type of weapon was on the main road. This is a vehicle that is able to roll with the launcher in the Bakovici of its load. The tactical reaction at this time could not have necessarily this type of weapon. So if it was possible to, for example, to burn a vehicle carrying this type of load, meant that they had this access to this type of weaponry. This indicated to me that most likely on the convoys coming from Croatia that there were weapons and there was ammunition on the convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who actually admitted to you that these supplies were coming from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Bradara himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said indeed he was very proud of the fact that supplies were coming from The republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When he explained what had happened to me he hardly tried to hide the smile on his face. You could see that he was a bit proud of what he was telling me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these supplies were being run through Bosnian Serb controlled territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through the south from the eastern direction to the west into the Kiseljak pocket, the same thing for Vares, Vares the convoys would go towards the north and towards the west to Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want to talk to you briefly about your second tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina which I think was from October of 1993 to May of 1994. What position did you occupy during your second tour with the Canadian battalion in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my second tour I was the senior liaison officer. I have five liaison officers who worked for me. The situation had changed, now there was a battalion that was there, see we go on shifts, rotation six-month rotations. The Canadian battalion had replaced mine and so I came Bakovici. But when I returned there were now good relations with the Bosnian Serbs and so we had daily contacts with the three fighting parties and there was also liaison with each of the factions. I had a fourth person who was working in Sarajevo and a fifth who would fill in any kind of holes that there were, if there were special liaison needs. But my main roll was to work with UNHCR to try to understand what were the humanitarian needs of the people and to present reports to them on safety situations, security situation, as far as knowing whether escorts were needed. This type of thing. This was one of my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 336. Now, during your second tour with whom were you liaising at HVO headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my second tour of duty the point of contact that was given to me at that moment in order to discuss all discussions with HVO was Kulacic (sic), Vinko Lucic was the name, he was the person who had came from the main headquarters of the Croatian army -- Bosnian Croatian army and he indicated to me that he was the person I had to meet with. I knew somewhat the structure at that moment. Ivica Rajic was at that time the commander, but he was no longer in Kiseljak. What I was told at that moment he had gone to Busovaca, but Mario Bradara was still there, I encountered him on one or two occasion during my tour of duty. We were not able to have meetings, we knew each other already, were able to greet one another. So Vinko Lucic was the person I met with on a daily basis or almost daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your understanding at this time was that Colonel Bradara was still overall operational zone commander in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My discussions with Lucic, yes, indicated to me that Colonel Bradara was still and he was still commander of the operational zone for central Bosnia for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could refer to the map that is in front of you and explain to the judges the tactical situation on the ground in the area of Fonjica when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to Bakovici up a little bit. During my first tour of duty in 1993 one of the things about Fonjica was the atmosphere that was there. Elsewhere it was quite obvious that there was fighting going on, but in Fonjica itself it was atmosphere which was altogether different. There seemed to be - it seemed to me that there had never been any fighting in Fonjica. When you went to Fonjica during the war you were not aware of war at all. Everyone was on their terraces and there were soldiers there, there were HVO soldiers both were present in the same city and there were no conflicts that were obvious. This is something that struck me at the beginning. This is something that was unique to Fonjica. And when I returned in October, 1993 the situation was completely different. At that time there was some fighting that had taken place and this had taken place in Fonjica, Fonjica city had been heavily damaged and I was told by officers of the battalion, the 2nd Royal Battalion who were there when I was not there explained to me that the Croatian forces of the HVO had to pull Bakovici to the south east. And when they pulled Bakovici they had burned several of the residents and some of the industries of Fonjica. In particular, in Fonjica there was a very large wood industry where wood was treated and used and cut into various materials and this was completely burned down. But the tactical situation that was at hand was quite graphical as you see on your screen. The BiH controlled part of the territory that was - can you still hear me when I move to this area - it was - it had HVO forces were in the southern area south of the blue line. They controlled the territory in the south. And, as I said, they did not look at this line as necessarily as a defensive line, but rather as a graphical representation. Now you had the BiH forces who were controlling, you see the green line, they were controlling what was north. So this is north of the Fonjica area which is controlled by the BiH. The reason why we use the little green line here this is particular example is one I used to explain the situation that we encountered when we went to Fonjica, which is not directly related but what is nonetheless important is that when this conflict took place in the Fonjica area there were two psychiatric hospitals there in the Fonjica area. The first, Adrine, which was located in No. 1 and then the other one is in Bakovici which is located near No. 2 on the map. Now these hospitals had young patients, children, handicapped persons physically and mentally. This is in the first No. 1 and at Bakovici you had adult patients and nonetheless, in all you had 400 or 500 patients in all in those two hospitals. Now when the combat broke out, the medical and civilian members, those persons supporting the staff here in these hospitals, immediately abandoned both hospitals. So in June, 1993 during one of the tours of the patrols, rather of the Canadian battalion we encountered these two hospitals and we saw that all the patients s had been left on their. Own at that time we intervened by giving each of the hospitals a platoon to deal with those two hospitals. The goal here was to try to help to maintain and save the lives of those patients who had been abandoned several days without food, without water, without any type of care or sanitation and the mental state of these patients was horrible, so we had to spend some days there to take care of them. From June, 1993 the Canadian battalion had a physical presence in these two hospitals. I'd say there was platoon size or maybe a little less than a platoon which is normally around 30 persons in a Canadian platoon and so we maintained our presence there until I left in May, 1994. We finally had a mill tear presence Canadian military presence in those two hospitals. And then we were there solely to deal with the patients we were there to watch them feed them, to help them and help to re-establish the buildings themselves so there was almost an entire company 23 if you will have men working on those two hospitals they played a certain roll and that was what the Canadian Battalion was able to accomplish as a mission in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that during the early part of November of 1993, the HVO launched an offensive northwards towards the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said that was importance of our presence there in the fields, the line blue -- the blue line represents approximately where the territory controlled by the HVO ends. So if you will, north-west. Now, you can see on the front line, I don't know whether it's visible on the screen, but if you look at the topographical lines, the terrain which is located behind Bakovici, or near Bakovici, shows that Bakovici is in the very bottom of the valley and you have an orange line that goes up to Sakovici, and there you see that it is located in a valley with two -- flanked rather by two mountains to the west and to the east. Now, if I recall correctly it was on second of November but definitely during the first week of February 1993 after our arrival because there was a relief that was made of the forces that was there on the 22nd and so on that evening there, there was still a platoon located there in the Bakovici hospital and the roll was there to deal with the patients. We also had observation posts and monitoring posts. Soldiers were responsible for making sure they could see what was going on or around their position. So they can maintain a certain level of security for the hospital. And also for the soldiers who were located there. In the evening, after we were installed, there was also - there was a offensive that was launched in the south-eastern part which went along the road towards the north and this offensive came from the HVO and for the first time they were using caterpillar vehicles. Now this is quite important because these were armoured vehicles with assault vehicles which are rarely seen in this part of Bosnia. On occasion one might see isolated cases of these kinds of vehicles but it was extremely rare. They do not see the actual armoured vehicle with their own eyes but they heard them coming and approaching. You can hear the sounds of these caterpillared vehicles, given the weight of these vehicles and the sound of the motors, for us it's something that's very easy to recognise. Because this type of vehicle is used by the Bosnian forces and would date back to the same type of vehicles used by the Soviet army. This is a type of clicking sound that is made by the sound of the caterpillar type of metal falling and moving forward. So it was quite easy to recognise for us. I am saying all of this to say at that moment there was an attack launched by the HVO force and we felt their purpose here was to move up the valley towards Fonjica in order to capture Fonjica. So during that attack the hospital which is located in the lower part of the valley gives an indirect way cover for those persons who you can see people who were advancing. So the hospital, if you will, could give you some degree of cover, and so indeed there was some HVO soldiers who penetrated the hospital and used it as a position from which they were able to open fire. At that moment the platoon was under control of Mr. Stevenson and his reaction was that, first of all, take the patients from the first floor and move them upstairs and also to remove the HVO soldiers not by force, but tell them that this is a hospital and it's unacceptable for them to use a hospital for a cover -- for the purposes of cover. And so they came to an agreement that the Bosnian forces no longer used the first floor but instead they still nonetheless used that building as cover in order to return fire from the Bosnian forces from the north-west. And so this is more or less what was happening at that time and there was also received a report later on that there were some chemical weapons that were used during that attack, but our investigation did not enable us to establish that indeed there were such weapons used. So this is a report, but I cannot confirm or not confirm whether or not such chemical weapons were use. There were no indications no clues that would tell us if such weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript it states that in fact Bosnian forces -- the Canadian soldiers came to agreement with the Bosnian soldiers to leave the hospital. Were they Bosnian government forces that occupied the hospital or HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what occurred is that our soldiers. The Canadian soldiers asked the HVO soldiers occupying ground level to leave the premises, so we asked them to leave the premises, this is a hospital, it is unacceptable for them to use a medical institution to defend yourself. And so this is what we asked the HVO soldiers to leave the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, this may be an appropriate time to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Well, we're going to resume at 2.30. ---Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. ---On resuming at 2.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume our hearing. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Learned Counsel. If the ELMO could be illuminated, please. Captain Lanthier, we've completed before lunchtime, your testimony concerning the use of the hospital at Bakovici, by the HVO, for covering concealment, whilst mounting a mechanised infantry attack north into Fonjica. I would now like you to tell the court about your knowledge of the use of patients within the hospital for proving routes through mine fields in the locality of Bakovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bakovici hospital and the property around it did not have a gate which could close things up completely, therefore it was natural for those patients outside who could -- that is, people who -- other people who wanted to go out of the hospital, it was normal for them to leave but that they would stay near the hospital, which meant that they could not be all watched over constantly. It was clear that the patients would go a little bit further than the immediate surroundings of the hospital, the actual compound itself of the hospital. I was told when we changed with the second battalion, that on some occasions, some of these patients had gone a little far from the hospital and they were taken by HVO soldiers and then they were used to verify whether there were mines around. It was a normal thing to use anti personnel mines in defence of position, and that was very frequent in Bosnia, but what happened is that some of the patients were taken by the HVO soldiers and asked to move, in a given direction, in order to check whether there were mines. If the patient could go forward without setting off a mine, then we knew that there was an opening, that is, a place that you could go through safely. But, if on the other hand, the patient set off a mine, first of all, the patient would be seriously wounded, if he wasn't killed, and then that was a way of proving that there was a mine field. It was a way, therefore, of detecting whether there was mine fields. This was reported to me by the group that had been there before us. And some of our soldiers who were there, told us about a time when a mentally handicapped patient, who was a little bit older, had been taken by the HVO soldiers, in fact, to check whether there was a mine field and the patient had set off the mine and had been killed. I went to Vinko Lucic with that report and asked that that kind of practise be stopped, that that kind of practise was completely inhumane. At that time, it was a practise that was being used, but -- that is the fact -- but he didn't consider very important that patients would set off mines. He didn't really clear. It was clear according to the report that I read from our soldiers in the hospital that it wasn't -- there weren't patients who had gotten lost, but who had accepted to go where the HVO soldiers had told them to go with the results that we know. So it was an absolutely inhumane practise but it was clear that they didn't care very much about it at all, that is on the level of the Kiseljak headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you reported this matter to Mr. Vinko Lucic at the headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that the staff of the Bakovici hospital, actually wished to return to it and to take care of the patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason I tried to do, which took up a lot of my time was to allow the civilian employees who had been working in the Bakovici hospital, and in the Drina hospital to go back. When I came there in the autumn of 1993, neither of the two hospitals had civilian employees working in them. That was the only -- the -- and the Canadian battalion had to take care of the patients. Once we were there, we would -- it was hard to take the patients to the hospital in Drina and in Bakovici. It was also very difficult because on several occasions, I tried to get the employees brought back. Bakovici was on the front-line as the blue line on the map shows. I negotiated the return of those employees with the former administrator of the Fojnica municipality, who was now living in Kiseljak, and who was responsible for those hospitals, particularly the Bakovici one. Since it was in HVO controlled territory. On several occasions, I was able to reach an agreement with him so that the employees would be able to come back and the agreement was that there would be a presence in the hospital, there would be fewer of them, but that there would be a section, not a platoon, and that there would be an armoured escort for those employees and we would go pick up the employees around 8.00 in the morning, and we would go cross the mountains taking the orange road, a road that went through the south, through the mountains. You can't see it on this map. We would go through the mountains and get to Bakovici. That was the agreement. But on two or three occasions, once we had reached an agreement, when the patrol came to Kiseljak to pick up the employees, the agreement wasn't honoured and without any explanation as to why an agreement which had been reached the night before was no longer being honoured the next morning, and I was told it was part of the hospital administrator's powers, that is, he was responsible for managing his own employees, but the clearer question was that the HVO refused to allow the employees to return to their work. This is an impression which formed in my mind when I heard the refusal on the part of the authorities about why they were not respecting the agreement and I thought that way we would have to talk about the whole thing all over again. That was the impression that I had, that they didn't want it to go through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could move ahead in time to the third week of January and I would like to describe to the court the events surrounding a humanitarian aid convoy which was bringing urgent medical supplies to the hospital in Bakovici. If you could recount that story to the court, from your initial agreement with the HVO in Kiseljak, through to the journey to Bakovici, and I believe that journey was the only route, marked orange on the ELMO, and you can refer to that in order to assist the judges in understanding your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could explain further the circumstances of the attack on the convoy. We maintained a presence in the Drina and Bakovici hospitals until I left in May 1994. The situation and the position of the forces on the ground means that the orange route, which originally was on the right side of your map, the orange road, we go from east to west, and at some point, I don't know if you can see it very clearly, but this section here, this part I'm showing on the map right here (indicating) is in the area which is in what's known as no-man's land, meaning no forces in control of it but which can be controlled by fire, either with light arms or with submachine guns. Since the route was very open to attacks, we recommended to UNHCR to give us the responsibility of bringing in the necessary commodities for the Bakovici hospital. UNHCR supplied the civilian vehicles as well as civilian soldiers, that is we decided we would bring in humanitarian assistance in our own vehicles, assistance to the Drina and Bacavici hospitals. In order for these convoys to pass, you needed prior authorisation from the Kiseljak headquarters, 24 hours in advance, at least. We had to go to the Kiseljak headquarters. We had to ask for authorisation to have the humanitarian assistance convoy and indicated each of the vehicles had to be present in the convoy to describe all the commodities and the amounts that would be brought in, that is the amounts -- it was mostly coal that we had there to heat up the two hospitals and also some food to bring in to feed the patients. Gasoline in order to have the generators operated, and both the hospitals used generators, coal generators, as well as medicine and other medical supplies that were required for the health of the patients. Therefore, we had to give details of all of this and then we would get written authorisation from Vinko Lucic which he would sign and which would then allow us to go through the various road blocks which were on the roads in order for us to go to the hospitals in Drina and Bakovici. What was peculiar to this road, it that it was located in no-man's land and controlled by firing. In fact, in each occasion that Canadian battalion vehicles used the road, there was shooting that came from the HVO positions. Personally, I came under that fire. Most of the time, it was firing that was being carried out in order to intimidate us. It wasn't -- it didn't hit my vehicle. I was in a 4 by 4, so they were just firing, but most of the time, one could see the shots exploding on the road, therefore it was very easy to see from where the firing was coming. Each time I complained, and I complained throughout my tour of duty, every time there was an attack, which was not justified and that was at the Kiseljak headquarters, and every single time the answer that was given to me is that these were isolated acts, that they were not authorised, and it was simply local initiatives of soldiers on the ground. A local initiative, perhaps, but the responsibility of the commander at that point should have been, if he had not authorised it, to make sure that his troops received the order to have this shooting stopped or to take out those of his superior officers who did not get the orders respected. When we come to the conclusion that this was not a local initiative, but that when one considered the commander was not doing his duty by stopping the attacks from being carried out. In any case, the major attacks against our soldiers were in the third week of January 1994, while a convoy, I think it was in the morning, was going from Kiseljak in order to bring -- supplies to both hospitals, and it came under HVO fire. At that point, the fire ordinarily was directed only at the armoured vehicles, that is, I had said that the non-armoured vehicles were often not -- were not being fired on where the armoured ones might have been fired on, and then the bullets would ricochet off. On that occasion, the non-armoured vehicles transporting humanitarian aid were also fired on. They were 'cougars' with turrets, there were cargo vehicles with humanitarian aid and they were well-known, because we received the written organisation for it to go through from Mr. Lucic, in order to send the materials through, and there was an ambulance convoy which was transporting the medical supplies and frequently, these medical supplies had to be refrigerated and the required vehicles for this were often the Red Cross ones. The convoy was attacked. It came under machine gun attack and then we lost two people -- had two casualties. The front part of the convoy was hit. The driver was hit two or three times in the foot but was able to take it on to Drina, and the other chauffeur did not lose control -- was not hit but he lost control of the vehicle which went off the road and that was a vehicle which was transporting diesel. We had to blow it up so that nobody else could use it later on because we didn't have the physical means in order to withdraw it, to pull out vehicles from ditches on the side of the road. At the time that the attack was reported to Mr. Lucic, there was a complaint made. We said it was an unjustified attack. We had been authorised to be there. This was mandatory aid for the patients in the two hospitals. The answer that Lucic gave was the same, once again, that it was a local initiative. It was something which he had not ordered and he denied that it had been ordered, but once again, in my opinion, he showed that he had not carried out his responsibilities because he knew very well that we were frequently prey to attacks and that he did not protect us from having this kind of attack happen again. It was this kind of attack that we experienced during the third week of January 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when you say that you dealt with Mr. Vinko Lucic at the Kiseljak headquarters and that you complained to Mr. Lucic at the Kiseljak headquarters, you're referring to the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lucic, as I said, was my contact point at the Kiseljak headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he, indeed, has authorised this convoy to travel the route from Kiseljak down to the Bakovici Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There was a checkpoint, which was at this point I'm showing you right here on the map (indicating); we were authorised to go to Bakovici and Drina without written authorisation for HVO. This was for the convoy, that is two armoured vehicles going through without any problems, without written authorisation, but when there was a convoy, one had to have the written authorisation from Mr. Lucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this convoy was prominently displaying the symbol of the international committee for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ambulance that was going with the convoy had the emblem of the Red Cross. There was no way of mistaking it for something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown an exhibit that's previously been admitted, which is Exhibit 80/5. Captain Lanthier, can you identify any of the individuals in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right is Mr. Vinko Lucic. There's Colonel Blaskic. I can't remember this man's name. I met him once. He was introduced to me as the commander of the Croatian army in Bosnia, that's the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man in the extreme right of the photograph is Mr. Vinko Lucic, next to his left is, of course, Colonel Blaskic, and the man to the left of Colonel Blaskic you only know as the commander of the Bosnia Croat forces in Bosnia. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What was the exact position -- what was his exact responsibility in relation to General Blaskic? What was Vinko Lucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had been introduced to him -- he himself introduced himself as the liaison officer of the HVO army headquarters in Mostar, and he answered to the Mostar headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving to the conclusion of your examination-in-chief, can you tell the Court what you know about the presence of organised Bosnian government forces in the municipality of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the Kiseljak pocket as such, there was no Bosnian government forces. The forces that were organised were not -- they were outside that pocket so there was no military formation within the Kiseljak pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Captain Lanthier, based exclusively on your knowledge of facts on the ground, can you describe to the Court the effectiveness of the HVO chain of command in the Vitez, Kiseljak and Vares areas from your experience in theatre during your two tours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chain of command on the HVO side seemed to be operating without any difficulty. Two specific examples that I can give you would be one of my first meetings with Colonel Blaskic, I explained why I wanted to introduce myself to him because there were problems -- in case of problems with Kiseljak, I could refer to him in order to solve the problems that I might be confronted with. I called upon him on two occasions, that I remember. I can't remember the details of the problems. I think they were related to something -- they had to do with freedom of movement in Kiseljak, and I thought that shouldn't have been a problem, so I went to see Colonel Blaskic about that. I remember -- this shows that the chain of command was operating because these situations were resolved once Colonel Blaskic intervened. As regards to the exercise of the chain of command, one of the basic criteria is communications, and the HVO had excellent communications among the various locations of its headquarters, particularly the presence of telephones and civilian lines, because the PPT building was under HVO control in Kiseljak and those telephone lines were working so they could use telephones to communicate. They could use faxes. I saw faxes in Kiseljak and in the Vares Hotel where the Vares brigade was located. <Svenko>, who was the deputy to the commander in Vares, he received a fax right in front of me. So you can see it was working. Also, that there were high frequency antennae, and there were also telephones that showed that there were satellite dishes on the roofs of the headquarters. I saw all of that and so they could see that there was a great deal of possibility to maintain communications among the various headquarters, which allowed the commander to exercise commander control over his troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your interpreter tell you about the communications capacities at the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the things that my interpreter at that particular time, in 1992, the interpreter was an army radio operator, so not only was he familiar with communications, but he also showed me the location of some of the antennas which were used by the headquarters. I, myself, was very familiar with the various frequencies used on the air waves, but he explained even more about the systems used in Bosnia on various occasions. The former Yugoslavia at that time had some of the best works of communication, as far as frequencies are concerned, in Europe, and definitely some of them were very well used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be accurate to say that, in your opinion, the tactical communications capacity of the HVO in central Bosnia was really very good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my opinion. That was confirmed, also, by observing the various types of communications equipment used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, speaking of physical links between Kiseljak and Vitez, are you aware of any rout from Kiseljak to Vitez which does not involve the use of the main road through Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there is one road or one path that does exist between Kiseljak and Vitez. I was fortunate to be able to have a good knowledge of the area in which I was working, and the road that I'm referring to is a dirt road which goes from the south of Vitez and goes down towards the south or south-east to go towards the east afterwards. With a four-wheel drive vehicle, one could take this dirt road, on this dirt road but on one occasion, I was able to use this road from Kiseljak to Vitez and the topographic map that I had was not -- rather, it was not of the same quality. In fact, very similar to what we have here, a photocopy, but none the less, I was able to find it just by chance using the various roads in the path because it's a very hilly area and would have to go through a forest -- through forests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a road which avoided having to use the main road from Vitez to Kiseljak that goes through Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you comment on the degree of cooperation that you received from the Bosnian government forces and the degree of cooperation that you received from the HVO? How would you compare the two during the nine months that you spent in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that the cooperation received from the BiH, from the Bosnian forces, government forces, were much better than those received from the HVO. As I said during my first tour of duty, in particular, I made daily visits to the Visoko headquarters, and there I would receive an overview of what was going on in the area which was under its control. This gave me a very good idea of what was going on, because our troops were not in a position to be able to be aware of everything that was going on in the sector, and so I was able to get some idea of what was going on. With the information that he would give me, I was then able to help me in my research and also see whether I could confirm what was in the reports. On one occasion, I was given a topographic map from the Bosnian army indicating all of their weapons, both in the HVO and the BiH army. At one time, I went to an exclusion zone. So, if you will, the cooperation from the BiH was good. With regards to the HVO, that was a little different, very different, in fact. Yes, it's true, we were not located in the same city, but I would move about on a daily basis to Kiseljak, either to talk to Mr. Bradara or Mr. Lucic, to talk about the various reports, but the discussions were never as productive. In order to obtain information, it seemed like I was pulling teeth. The information that was given to me would often not correspond to what I could have deduced from looking at what had happened. I can give you several examples. I gave you a few examples earlier this morning. As far as cooperation was concerned, that was quite different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, and referring particularly to the time of your service in April of 1993, what is your professional opinion of the military operation that you saw taking place in Vitez and Kiseljak during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my mind, it was clear, and even more so in retrospect, that the operations that were carried out in the Vitez and Kiseljak pockets constituted ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population living there. They were carried out in the military fashion. The tactics utilised and the use of the land and all the other factors, which I've already mentioned, indicates quite clearly that these were not -- that one day to the next, a farmer decides to exterminate his neighbours, but rather a systematic extermination, or an attempt at a systematic extermination through an organised force or a synchronised force. When you look at what happened in Vitez two days later, this thing continued in the Kiseljak pocket, and then several days later, in Breza, in this 302nd bigrade, I was told that the same thing was being prepared for Vares and Stupnido. And I was told by this brigade that he feared for Stupnido. History showed later on that the exact same thing was to happen there. So it was systematic, it was organised, and there was no doubt whatsoever that this was a military operation against a civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain Lanthier. I have no further questions. If I can apply for admission into evidence of exhibits 329 through to 336, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are there any observations from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Only one, Mr. President. 329?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a municipality that is darkened in that was not within the CANBAT area of responsibility, the Busovaca municipality, and the witness has testified that all the darkened municipalities were within the CANBAT area of responsibility. So I would ask the witness mark through that municipality and initial it or something or that the map otherwise be altered prior to admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think actually the point of the testimony of the witness was to not only indicate the areas of responsibility, but I think he also indicated that they were municipalities that he actually travelled in. I would suggest to the Court that the map does not need any form of amendment and can be admitted as it is. If there's a dispute, perhaps the witness then can be asked to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think it's quite easy to resolve. These are problems which are not real, true problems. I think Mr. Hayman made an observation that it is marked on the transcript as such, and we are going to then allow for these documents to be admitted as such. Mr. Hayman, are you going to be entering the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, you are now going to receive questions being put to you by Mr. Hayman who is one of the Defence Counsel for General Blaskic. Mr. Hayman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your first tour of duty in Bosnia, were you the liaison officer for CANBAT in your sector or were you the deputy liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the liaison officer for the warring factions and not the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So did you have a staff of liaison officers below you as you did during your second tour, or did you have some other position during your first tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my first tour, I was the only liaison officer for the warring factions; therefore, I did not have any staff or other liaison officers working under my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say the liaison officer for the warring factions, was there any other liaison officer for CANBAT during your first tour, other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One other individual had two functions. Mr. Lambert was also there as a liaison officer. Once a week, he will go to the UNHCR in order to sometimes give briefings to the UNHCR. That was the role of the liaison in the sense that he also coordinated with people outside of his own unit but no contact with the warring factions was involved. So I was the only, the sole warring factions liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, when you receive questions, of course it's quite normal that you would face the defence. However, when you respond, it is also equally normal that you face the judges. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you were the only liaison officer for the warring parties and that you had sole responsibility for the Koscan, Vares Visoko, and Kiseljak, Fojnica, Kresevo areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as liaison activities, yes, but I was not the only person in the field. The responsibility of the tactical officer in the UNHCR was also to go into the field and to cover the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you were the only liaison officer whose charge it was to maintain contact with the warring parties in the municipalities I listed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. I was the initial appointed liaison, but I'm sure that once a liaison is established at the location of the other headquarters within the area of responsibility would then be disclosed to all the members within this tactical group. For example, if someone is going to be with a convoy, escorting a convoy, and they encounter a problem, I cannot intervene to help. That person would then go to the headquarters to speak with a member of that particular headquarters. And so I'm not the only person who would have a direct contact with the members of the headquarters in that area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it, then, it's more accurate to say you were the only full-time liaison officer for the warring parties in the municipalities I listed; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said you arrived in Visoko in mid-February 1993. How long thereafter did you first visit the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have taken a week, so near the end of February, I say, or even perhaps towards the early part of March. I'm saying approximately, I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 330 could be provided and placed on the ELMO, that would be helpful, Mr. President. You relayed a briefing or a discussion you had with Mr. Bradara in the course of your first meeting or visit to the Kiseljak barracks. Is it correct that as a liaison officer, one of your functions was to familiarise yourself with who were the commanders in the field with whom one would conduct a liaison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said approximately what I expressed in my testimony earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have identified the Bobovac brigade as being the HVO unit in Vares. Can you tell us who the commander was of that brigade at any time during your tours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Emil Arah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that during your first tour, your second tour, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that it was, indeed, during my first tour of duty, but right now I do not remember whether or not during my second tour of duty he was still there. At that time, I was no longer the warring factions liaison officer, but rather added to the UNHCR. My role was different then. So then the line of command was not as clear in all cases, especially since from our arrival in Vares, as I remember, it was attacked by the BiH, and so Stupni did fall. And at that time, that's one of the reasons I have no real clear memory of what that line of command was in that area. I was not quite clear of the name of the commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And did you ever learn that after the massacre at Stupni do, Emil Arah or Hares, as you have called him, was removed as the brigade commander of the HVO in Vares. Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I cannot recall with any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You cannot recall with detail. Can you recall anything concerning that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the Stupni do, after the Stupni do massacre, we were not able to carry out any detailed investigation escorted by the tactical groups. As far as most of the details are concerned, I received a report from Ivica Rajic about Stupni do, but as far as the other details are concerned, it was at the very early part of our arrival there, so I wasn't able to get an idea of the field there, so really the details I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Stupni do fell. Did you mean that the HVO unit in Vares was expelled and the BiH army second corps took control of Vares in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Attack was carried out by the BiH and the city was, in part, captured by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that in approximately December 1993, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was earlier than that. It was, rather, in November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to the Kiseljak municipality. When you first met with Ivica Rajic, the Commander, as you've described him, of the Ban Jelacic Brigade and we'll refer to Mr. Bradara, did you learn or were you told how long or for what period of time Ivica Rajic had been the brigade commander in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think I said that Mr. Rajic was the commander of the brigade in Kiseljak. I think what I stated that he was the commander of the headquarters which was located in Kiseljak, and that under his command, he had four units. We don't see it on the screen now, but Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, and Vares. As far as Ban Jelacic, I'm sorry, the name comes to mind, I'm not sure whether it was Ban Jelacic, but in any case, it wasn't Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I stand corrected in terms of your characterisation of your testimony. So your testimony is that Rajic was not the brigade commander; he was only the operational group commander in Kiseljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who the brigade commander was in late February or early March 1993 when you first visited the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I just told you, I'm not certain of the name. The name of Mijo Bosic came to mind, but I can't tell you that indeed this is the name of the commander, but my relation, given the fact that this was a headquarters that was above Kiseljak and controlled all of the HVOs in the area of responsibility, I was not called upon to work directly with the commanders of the brigades or units, if you will, beneath them. I worked principally with Mr. Bradara, who was a deputy commander to Rajic. And that's why all the operational groups underneath Rajic I did encounter from time to time, once or twice, especially in Vares, because Vares was much more isolated in a way; not completely isolated, but more so. And this is why the commanders from Fojnica, Kresevo, and Kiseljak's names escape me for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does the name Mijo Bosic mean anything to you in connection with the brigade commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it twice. This is a name that comes to mind. Perhaps my pronunciation is incorrect, but I've used this name twice already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does it come to mind in any connection, such as the commander of the brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please ask your question more directly, Mr. Hayman. These are the type of questions which are so subtle, that perhaps it would be better, since you're dealing here with judges, I think it is better that you ask the question directly, otherwise you seem to be wasting a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Captain, did you ever hear that Mijo Bosic was the brigade commander of the HVO brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the third time, I will repeat that the name escapes me, but I'm associating the name of Mijo Bosic to the commander of the Ban Jelacic brigade. I don't know if he was, indeed, the commander, but this is the name that comes to mind. This is the third time you've asked me this question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Mr. Bradara had become the brigade commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mario Bradara was never introduced to me as the commander of the Kiseljak brigade. He was introduced to me as the deputy commander for the operation of the group for Kiseljak, and it was in this capacity that I carried out my meetings with him. If at one time or another he changed his post, this was not indicated to me in my meetings with him during my first tour of duty. It was in his capacity as deputy commander that I had dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Ivica Rajic had taken the post of brigade commander in addition to the post of commander of the operational group based in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To understand the question correctly, you're asking whether or not he had two roles, the commander of the operational group and also the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you, did you ever hear in May, April or May, of 1993 that Ivica Rajic had taken on dual positions as brigade commander and commander of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This information was not given to me, if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, in Visoko, was there an HVO unit in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no unit there, not during my time, not the HVO unit in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What 'corpus' or 'corps' of the BiH army was in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an operational group there in Visoko. It was subordinate to the headquarters which was located in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were units of the first corps of the BiH army based in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must be careful in answering that question, because when we talk about a unit which belongs to a particular corps, it's difficult to say whether or not this is under an operational group, because this is a group that's responsible to its higher headquarters. A unit that belongs to its first corps is within the chain of command, you must go directly to ISTOK. And then I must respond directly to the other lower subordinate -- I'm not sure whether -- you can ask your question differently to see if I understand you correctly, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why don't I rephrase it. Was the first corps of the BiH army based in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first corps was in Sarajevo, and the ISTOK responded to the first corps located in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Part of your answer is being translated. Perhaps it's operational group, OG ISTOK, I'm not sure what it is. It is not comprehensible to me. Can you assist me in understanding what unit or group you're identifying in Visoko. Is that operational group ISTOK, I-S-T-O-K?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In Fojnica, there was an HVO brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a group or a unit, as I indicated earlier, Fojnica was quite unique during my first tour of duty in that there was an absence of war in Fojnica and that was quite clear. So I was not called upon to work a great deal with the commander for the units or groups located in Fojnica. I only met with him once and his name escapes me. For a battalion or a brigade, I'm not really in a position to tell you what was the size of the troops in Fojnica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Mijo Bosic ever become the HVO commander in Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Mario Bradara ever become the HVO brigade commander, or other commander of HVO unit or units in Fojnica, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he was, he never informed me of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, between when you left the theatre after your first tour and returned during your second tour, the HVO was expelled from Fojnica, correct, and the BiH army took control of Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a situation that corresponded to my arrival in October 1993. I was told that there had been fighting in the area and that Fojnica now was controlled by the government, the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you also told that approximately 6,000 Croats had been displaced from Fojnica as a result of that conflict in Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as the numbers are concerned, that escapes me once again. My role at that moment was no longer a role as in liaison officer in the field. At that moment, I was working primarily with the UNHCR for most of the time. What I can, perhaps, do is if there was warring -- a war going on there, then during a war, it was quite often to have a movement of population in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Vares an HVO enclave prior to its fall to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one of the HVO enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Kiseljak, was Kiseljak, after you arrived -- well, after January of 1993 and thus prior to your arrival in February 1993, was Kiseljak also an HVO enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Kiseljak pocket was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that pocket was surrounded, was it not, by the BiH army and, in one part, the Bosnian-Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the Vitez Busovaca pocket, that also was an enclave, was it not, surrounded by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated on exhibit 330 two other operational groups. If you don't know, please say so, I won't belabour the point. But was Maglaj also a location under the command of the operational zone, central Bosnia, and was it also an HVO enclave prior to its fall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't really know now. Five years have passed, I don't remember. Since Maglaj wasn't in my sector, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand completely. How about Zepca, do you know whether Zepca was also an HVO enclave within the central Bosnian operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, but once again, I have to say that my memory is not good enough to be able to tell you with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lastly, Usora, was that also an HVO enclave within the central Bosnian operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Between these various enclaves, those that you've identified, did you personally, yourself, see BiH army units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to be sure I understand your question. Is it whether the BiH forces were completely surrounding those enclaves? Is that the question you're asking? Is that the sense of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll make it more precise. For example, between the Kiseljak enclave and the Vitez Busovaca enclave, did you yourself see the BiH army units that were separating those two enclaves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the ground -- there were Bosnian government forces on the ground, but there was not a continuous line or with complete defensive positions surrounding a region. 'Civilous' I think is the word that is used in English for that. For example, at Kacuni and Bilalovac - on the main road from Busovaca to Kiseljak - did you, yourself, observe front-line positions between the HVO and the BiH army in each of those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, possibly. I don't remember where, as soon as I arrived, those positions were, in fact. I know the Busovaca and Kiseljak, it was Bilalovac and Kacuni they cut the road and, by definition, the road then became a main road -- one of the roads that you could go through. I remember this because when I was in Washington corps, one of the purposes of the battalion came to patrol the front lines, and I know that in April of 1994, there were Bilalovac positions in Kacuni. But earlier than that, I really couldn't tell you whether there were defensive positions, whether there had been anything that had been dug out at those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you transit that road, the main road from Busovaca to Kiseljak during either of your tours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I said in my testimony this morning, this was a road that I took many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And were there BiH army checkpoints or barricades on that road at both Bilalovac -- the area of Bilalovac and the area of Kacuni when you transited that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were. At what time they came, whether it was the beginning of my tour, I'm not really quite sure as to the time that these checkpoints existed. But when I was there, there were checkpoints that existed in Kacuni and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar if 330 is on the ELMO and if it could be activated, please? Thank you. On Exhibit 330, it is indicated that Franjo Nakic was the deputy commander of the operational zone. Where did you get that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the first time that I met Mr. Nakic it was during a meeting for the joint Busovaca commission, if I'm not mistaken. I think it was as such that he was introduced to me, if I remember correctly. That was the time that I -- that his role was introduced to me, or that explained to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Outside of the protocols and formal introductions at the Busovaca joint commission, did anyone ever tell you that Franjo Nakic was the deputy commander to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember I met Mr. Nakic at the Hotel Vitez I believe, although I'm not sure. I think that he was present during one of my meetings with Colonel Blaskic, but the details are a bit fuzzy in my mind now. But I met him several times, and I do remember that I met him in Busovaca and in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You told us of a visit to Colonel Blaskic, a courtesy call, if you will, to introduce yourself. Is that a fair characterisation of the visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Courtesy call, if you like. The purpose was to introduce me -- to introduce myself, introduce the Canadian battalion, which had just come in, along with UNPROFOR in central Bosnia and which was working in a part of the area which is under HVO control. It was a bit more than a courtesy call, it was more to establish more specific relations and not merely to introduce myself to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When was that visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it must have been the first week of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you went to Vitez to see him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that because you knew his headquarters was in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The British officer who was responsible for liaison in the region before I arrived, as I said this morning, had identified the positions of the various headquarters. And since we were rather close to the Vitez headquarters--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think the interpreter missed a bit of the answer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The answer ends, 'and since we were rather close to the Vitez headquarters'. Do you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter made a mistake there, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The British corps was close to the -- he showed me where the HVO headquarters were in Vitez. Because it wasn't the Canadian camp that was there but the British one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the BRITBAT liaison officer tell you that Colonel Blaskic's headquarters was in the Hotel Vitez in Vitez, in roughly March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He showed me the place. I don't remember whether at that point he identified by name Colonel Blaskic. But this was all very quickly -- this was done very quickly. He explained all the responsibilities that were involved during the course of one day. So I don't -- I'm not sure whether he mentioned the name specifically of Colonel Blaskic as the commander of the operational zone of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The conversation you had with Colonel Blaskic in, I believe you said, the first week of March, 1993, was that with the benefit of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since my knowledge of the Serb/ Croatian language was zero, I worked with an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you discussed the subject in general terms - and I'm not characterising your testimony - the area of responsibility; that is, the area of responsibility within the operational zone of central Bosnia. Do you remember what term or terms precisely were used to characterise his area of responsibility? Was it area of responsibility? Was it command? Was it control? What term or terms were actually used, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards the exact terms, I couldn't tell you. I can't tell you the specific terms that we used. I'm familiar with the general concept. As far as certain specific terms that we used, no, I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you take any notes? Do you have anything to refresh your recollection so that you could be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. I say unfortunately, because, as I was saying, we were rotations, and so each meeting that I was present at there were notes taken on it, and then there was an information sheet, and when I left, it was natural to give the notebook with the information sheets in it to the next person. So the notes were exchanged, but my own notebook was not kept, and when I came back in October, 1993 for my second tour, I was not able to get my notebook back. So, no, I do not have any notes anymore which give detailed descriptions of my conversations and meetings with all of the people that I might have met during my stay in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the course of this conversation, did you discuss with Colonel Blaskic the difficulties involved in being responsible for an area that included enclaves in Vitez Busovaca, the Kiseljak enclave, the Vares enclave and, perhaps, the other enclaves in Kiseljak and Busovaca. Did you discuss that topic with him at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that time, he did not tell me that he was experiencing any difficulties in controlling those enclaves. Perhaps it would be the opposite, in fact. He said that his door was open if I needed to see him again, not to hesitate to come back to see him and -- or make an appointment and come back to see him. And if he wasn't in Kiseljak, then I could see him elsewhere. If he could, he would help me to solve any problems that might have come about in Kiseljak. This seemed to me that he was in a position to exercise command and control of the various formations that were under his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand he said that his door was open to you, but did you discuss the subject with him of what was involved in commanding an area that was broken up into four or five or more isolated enclaves? Did you discuss that subject matter with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. The question has now been asked twice. The witness has answered the question. Mr. Hayman has expressed it very clearly and the witness has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He answered that Colonel Blaskic said that 'my door would always be open to you'. He didn't say whether or not this subject was discussed. If it was, fine; if it wasn't, fine. I just would like an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, he answered you. He answered you very specifically. Maybe he answered you in a way that you don't like, but he did answer. He said that the problem was not brought up, but what Colonel Blaskic did say was something that would make him think that Colonel Blaskic had certain manoeuvrability and I think that was clear then. You can move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll move on. My translation was not as clear as Your Honour indicated, but I'm pleased that the answer was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's the role of the presiding judge in order to clarify interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President. My colleague indicates there was something in the transcript about General Blaskic being in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You met him in Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to say, that I had gone to Vitez to meet Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Turning to the Busovaca joint commission, do you know why it was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Busovaca commission was established before I arrived. The specific purpose of the commission was not explained to me in a very specific manner. What I was able to deduce from my involvement was that it was -- one of the objectives that I noticed at that time was that we tried to establish some kind of normality within the region, and I remember that there were discussions about military, economic and social matters. The very nature and the exact mandate of the commission, the joint Busovaca commission is something that I don't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where were the meetings of the Busovaca joint commission, that you attended, held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one that I attended was in the Busovaca region. I can't give you the exact place. It was, I remember, in Busovaca, but exactly where I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you attend other meetings of the commission in other places, or were all the meetings you attended in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really tell you whether it was a meeting of the commission or the coordination committee, but I do remember there was a meeting which took place in Vitez. I don't know which meeting it was, but I remember there was a meeting in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic participate in these meetings? Did he speak at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, as I said, was not present in Busovaca. It was Nakic who was there. The other meeting, which was called the coordinating committee. There Colonel Blaskic was there along with Colonel Stewart as the commander of the British battalion, and during that meeting Colonel Blaskic spoke several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we will now take a break, Mr. Hayman. About how much longer do you have, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think I'm about halfway through, Mr. President, halfway through my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a 20-minute break. ---Recess taken at 3.50 p.m. ---On resuming at 3:50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Captain, you were describing before the break that there was a meeting at which Colonel Stewart attended, Colonel Blaskic attended, and you believed it might be a coordinating committee meeting and you also attended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there any other meetings, that is, formal meetings such as of the Busovaca joint commission or other formal group meetings that you attended at which Colonel Blaskic also attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aside from what I've said to you about the several meetings I attended, I don't remember having attended any others where Colonel Blaskic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The coordination committee meeting you've described, is that the meeting where also Mr. Kordic was also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At this meeting, do you remember what Colonel Blaskic said, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I think that he spoke several times, but just exactly what he said and the specific subjects that were spoken about, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, I believe you said you understood Mr. Kordic to be a political advisor to Colonel Blaskic. Is that your understanding or opinion or was that the understanding or opinion of your interpreter which that person relayed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's my own opinion. As I said, I was not an active member of the commission, I was a back bencher, as we say in English, so I would go through my interpreter to know what was being said during the discussions. She interpreted for me, that was what she was supposed to do. Since I had -- Dario Kordic had been presented to me as one of the political leaders of the HVO in central Bosnia, the impression that I formed was that Mr. Kordic, when he would advise Colonel Blaskic or speak to him, that he would -- acted as a sort of political advisor. That's the personally opinion that I formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you formed this based on seeing them together at one or more meetings; is that right, formed this opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I went to two or three meetings and what was said and what my interpreter interpreted for me allowed me to form that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So at how many meetings did you see both Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, two or three times, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were those Busovaca joint commission meetings or some kind of other meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I also said, it was under the umbrella -- I don't think that they were the very meetings of the Busovaca joint commission, but rather on a higher level. But I don't have the exact name. I think it was the coordinating committee. I think that was the name of the meetings. But I really can't guarantee you that 100 percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything that Colonel Blaskic said at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's too long ago. Just what was said is not something I can remember now. I can remember the ideas, the concepts, and what the people represented in my opinion then, that was why I used the words I used in my statement and described the people as I did, often in general terms, because I remembered the concepts, but not the specific locations or the specific addresses or the exact words that were said. You're talking about something that went on more than five years ago now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about what was said between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic at any of the meetings that were attended by both of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
