utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, please move to another question. It's been 10 minutes now that we're trying to learn what Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kordic said. What are you trying to do? Are you trying to destabilise the witness? He's answered everything he can answer. Please, change your questions. We know what was said, we know what the witness can remember, what he can't remember. Try to move forward. You're working with professional judges. We understand. We're listening. Please, move to another question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 80-9? Could it be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Captain, could you look at 80-9 and tell us if you see Mr. Kordic in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's who it is (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Can we have a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's who it is. .

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can we have a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It didn't come through on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could turn back to the microphone so the interpreter can pick up your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This individual I'm pointing to with the pointer, I think that's Mr. Kordic. As I said, I only met him several times and they were not personally conversations I had with him. So I know the name very well, and I did meet him, but as an individual and what he looked like, I think that's Mr. Kordic, but I really can't tell you that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indicating for the record, Mr. President, the witness has indicated the camouflaged individual who is the third person from the far right of the exhibit immediately behind two men who are not in uniform, in striped -- vertically striped shirts. We're done with that exhibit, Mr. Registrar, thank you. Turning to the 17th of April, 1993, you said you had a conversation with a BiH army commander in Visoko concerning the conflict in Vitez. Did he tell you that he had received information up the chain of command within the BiH army concerning this conflict in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was speaking in the morning with the -- with Memisevic, he told us that he heard there was fighting in Vitez, but he didn't know whether they were subordinate formations or whether they were on a higher level. He simply said to me that something was going on and he noted it for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you went to see or to attempt to see Colonel Blaskic on either the 18th or 19th of April, 1993, and you went to Vitez to try and see him; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you make an appointment before you went? Did you call before you went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I think I said, there was no telephone line from Visoko that was operational with Vitez, so I couldn't make an appointment. Yes, it's true that Colonel Blaskic had told me not to hesitate to make an appointment, but it wasn't easy, given the situation, it wasn't so easy to make appointments with Colonel Blaskic before going to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Speaking of telephone lines, did the telephone line from Vitez to Kiseljak run through Kacuni and Bilalovac, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the telephone lines were located. That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether from a Vitez phone you could telephone Kiseljak during your tours of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina or vice-versa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The telephone lines, as far as I know were operating, and when he met him in the beginning of March, he was the one who used the telephone to make the appointment with Colonel Blaskic which showed me, at that time, there was telephone connection and that the telephone was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you went back to try and see Colonel Blaskic again. When was that; was it the next day, two days later? Can you help us pinpoint that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, the first time was the 18th and so it must have been the 19th that I went back to Vitez. The 18th or 19th, it was two days in a row. I think it was the 18th and 19th, but maybe it was the 17th and 18th, or maybe the 18th and 19th. It was two days in a row. It wasn't a day afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you call ahead to try and make an appointment on the second occasion when you went back, or did you just go and try to get a meeting after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the telephone wasn't working the next day either, I couldn't make an appointment and so I just went to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, you told us you went from Visoko to Kiseljak and you went through Busovaca which was, we might call, the northerly route; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We would go from Visoko, go up and then go to the south-east toward Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why did you go that route as opposed to going straight down from Visoko and in through Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said this morning that according to what Mr. Memisevic's report gave to me, said that r had been similar attacks in the Kiseljak pocket, and I didn't want to go to the headquarters in Kiseljak saying that BiH forces told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why did you do that, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My approach was to go on site in order to confirm or not to confirm what had happened before going to the Kiseljak headquarters to ask questions about things that they wouldn't have known. But I wanted to confirm -- Mr. Memisevic's report would see to be correct, and that's when I met Mr. Bradara in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you saw a machine gun firing into a house or houses on that occasion. Do you remember what village that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village, the exact village, I don't remember, but it was right north-west of the city of Kiseljak. The picture's in my head, it was a rather open land and it would rise towards the east and the machine-guns would fire towards the north-west. But I can't tell you the exact name of the village. It was open ground north-west of Kiseljak, north of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For how long did you observe this activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't remain in those positions. I could see that there was, in fact, firing, shooting going on. I continued the road to the headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 333 could be provided to the witness and, perhaps, put on the ELMO? I'm turning your attention to the 20th of April, 1993. You said you were first taken to Borina. Is Borina on higher ground than Rotilj, itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, yes, because I think I remember -- or it seems I went down a hill with Colonel Landry when I was going toward Rotilj. Therefore, as I recall, yes, Borina was higher up, but I would have to look on a map in order to know more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many persons were you told by the Muslim inhabitants of Rotilj had been killed in the recent attack or conflict that had occurred there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm understanding the question. Could you repeat it for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many persons were you told by the Muslim inhabitants of Rotilj had been killed in the recent attack or conflict that had occurred in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that it was 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you talk to any Croat inhabitants of Rotilj during your visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the people who came to speak to me didn't say hello, I'm a Croatian, this is what happened. The people who came to me just said that -- just described what had happened to their families or to the people that they knew in the village of Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told by anyone on that occasion whether any Croats had been killed in the course of the conflict that had recently occurred in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody told me that there were any Croats who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that r had been a number of military-aged Muslim males in the village who had possessed something in excess of 50 rifles prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I got that question, that they had 50 weapons, is that what you asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You went and you spoke to a number of residents in Rotilj. Did any of them tell you that r had been a number of military-aged men of Muslim ethnicity in Rotilj prior to the conflict in possession of upwards of 50 or more rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I understand. Yes, I was told that there were men who were of fighting age, that is, who could fight, but I was not told that they had weapons. After having spent 13 months in Bosnia and Croatia, I know that many of the residents, a great majority of the residents had weapons, whether they were hunting weapons or other kinds of weapons. That was frequent but I was never told that there were men who had caches of arms in Rotilj. So I was not told that Rotilj was a possible military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told by any inhabitants that r had been negotiations between representatives of the village and the HVO over the surrender of those weapons that the villagers had possessed? Did anyone mention that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was never told, neither by the inhabitants who were there, nor by Mario Bradara. When I spoke to him, he never indicated to me that r had been any type of a talk about this, when this was attacked. This is something that never came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us in circle 2 on Exhibit 333, approximately how many burned houses did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall how many houses, exactly. If you look at the photo, perhaps you might try to deduce the number of houses. To my memory, there's a certain number, but I cannot tell you an exact number in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you estimate? If you can't, just tell us. I'm not trying to force you into a figure, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has indicated what his answer is to this question. He can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cayley, not exactly, otherwise I would have stopped Mr. Hayman before he made the question. He's asking for a basic estimation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I can't tell you how many houses -- what I can say is that in circle 2, most of them were affected, while in circle 3 not all of them were. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that there were hundreds of houses in the village as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hundreds seem to be quite a high number. I can look at the photograph in more detail, but that seems a bit high. I can't give you the number of houses which are there in the entire village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 334 could be provided to the witness. You indicated that on the 21st or 22nd of April, 1993, you visited the villages that are indicated on Exhibit 334. Now, excluding the village of Rotilj, which we've already discussed, I believe I heard you properly, but I want to make sure, that there were no residents residing in any of the other five villages marked on 334 at the time you visited them on the 21st or 22nd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the houses that I saw and the places where I visited, except the north of Gromiljak, I did not encounter anyone in the houses, in the places that I visited. I did not go into each house. You should understand that at that time that even if the attack was no longer underway, I was a target of fire and once in awhile I had to hide in some stables in order to avoid attacks. So this was not an easy task to go out and inspect this village. I saw what I saw and I did not see any sign of life, other than those of livestock, which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us with respect to the five villages indicated on 334, excluding Rotilj, what proportion or what rough percentage of houses were burned on the occasion that you visited them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very large percentage. I cannot give you an exact percentage point, but I would say a great majority of them were affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In each of those five villages, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge. Perhaps if you look at an in aerial photo, you might have a better idea of how many were actually affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you went to see Mr. Bradara after this inspection and had a discussion with him and he gave you explanations that you found unsatisfactory. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps inspection is a bit strong. I did not inspect, as such, rather I noted by looking and as noted, as you stated, Mr. Bradara's explanation seemed to me to be quite improbable. This is my opinion based on our meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any information concerning on what the Kiseljak brigade or the operative group in Kiseljak may have reported to Colonel Blaskic concerning events in the Kiseljak municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understand your question. Are you asking me if I was aware of what the Kiseljak headquarters responded to Vitez? Is that what you're saying? I would like to be able to understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll restate it. My question is, do you have any information concerning what the Kiseljak brigade or the operative group may have reported up the chain of command to Colonel Blaskic concerning these events, given Mr. Bradara's response to you concerning -- that these events were localised, unrelated incidents committed by frustrated citizens or what have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have not seen any report about what was communicated up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you visited Rotilj later on on a weekly basis. Was that during your second tour or during your first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was during my first tour of duty, during the events that took place around, let's say, the 18th of April. In the week that followed, I began to carry out weekly visits in Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether, by the time of your second visit were the residents of Rotilj receiving regular food assistance from Caritas and/or Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't tell you which organisation provided humanitarian relief, whether it was Merhamet the Muslin group or Caritas. I'm not in a position to say so. As far as the quantity of humanitarian aid, I'm really unable to say how much was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the Kiseljak barracks, did you see any detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the detainees. Well, let me back up. I saw children who were playing in the grounds in front, whether or not they were detainees, my impression was they were detainees, indeed. What Mr. Bradara informed me, that they were being detained for their security. I saw children outside. I saw other signs, however, to use the English expression, tell-tale signs that indicated the presence of women in the Kiseljak barracks. So I only saw children, but Mr. Bradara admitted that for their own security, according to him, these persons were detained in the Kiseljak barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described the wealth of supplies and, indeed, even luxuries in the Kiseljak enclave. Did you find the conditions different in the Vitez Busovaca enclave during your first tour when you visited that enclave; that is, with respect to the availability of supplies and the low cost of gasoline, cigarettes, chocolate and the like which you found in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Busovaca, because this was not within my area of responsibility, I travelled through Busovaca, but I never stopped there except for the few meetings I mentioned to you, and I did not carry on liaisons with either civilian or military persons there, but to the best of my memory, don't forget I spent very, very little time there, but to state precisely, I really can't tell you whether Busovaca was as good a situation as Kiseljak. I would say no, but it's very unclear in my mind right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the court whether there was any piece of territory controlled by the Bosnian-Serb army that was adjacent to the Vitez Busovaca enclave and whether there was such a piece of territory adjacent to the Kiseljak enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, in the eastern part, definitely not, but in the western part, I'm trying to visualise myself, the front-lines there. I don't know if -- not to my knowledge, not to my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information or reports concerning who profited from the sale of petroleum products or other smuggled goods to the Bosnia-Serbs? That is, who within the Kiseljak pocket profited from that activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not prepared to say this is a contraband; to say as far as who benefited from this, unless there was someone who gathered the money from what was sold, and I'm not in a position to say so, but this was much more than simple contraband. This was something that was organised by the authorities and this was not only something that was brought -- hidden from the authorities, it was something that was quite sanctioned by them and Mr. Bradara told me quite clearly that this was known and quite sanctioned. If they had been contraband, it would not have been sanctioned. That's the impression I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to the second tour and the situation you described in and around Fojnica. With respect to these two hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, had they been under civilian administration or military administration as of the first time that relevant events were brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were under civilian authority. There was a civilian manager there in each hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were not present when the initial fall, if you will, of Fojnica to the BiH army occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's right. That happened as it was reported to me in the spring of 199 -- the beginning of summer, 1993. At the time, I was in Canada, but it was during a briefing that I received about what was going on as the post was passed on in October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said there were some houses burned in the course of those events. Do you know, were those Muslim homes or Croat homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. All I know is what was told to me is that there were houses that were burned by Croatian forces. I will not venture so far as to say who owned these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, later in November when you've described additional difficulties, if you will, at the hospitals, were you there or did you receive reports from others concerning these activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're referring to the attack or the offensive that was launched by the HVO in the early part of November, I was not there. That was during the evening. We had Canadian troops which were under the command of UNPROFOR, but given the importance of what was happening there and the situation on the ground, I was in the regimental command post which is in direct contact with the troops and so I was able to follow the development of the situation there. The reason why I was not -- the reason why I went directly to the place, is because I needed to try and get a complete report of what was going on there. So if need be, I could go to Kiseljak to get a more detailed report. But, of course, to travel that even would be difficult. There's only one time in which we did so. I don't remember exactly -- what I can say is I was in a position to be able to follow on the radio the various events that took place as they were reported to us by the persons, the commanders who were there on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Again, my question was very simple. Were you there? I'll ask you another short question and ask you to focus on it to the best of your ability. Did you ever go, during the November offensive, to the hospitals or go with any of the convoys that were attacked? Do you have any personally knowledge of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it with my own eyes, the attack. I don't have personally knowledge, but I saw the reports and heard their voices on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were the reports of these events that you received written or oral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, these were verbal. Perhaps, I don't know, it's a bit vague. Maybe I should explain the communication. This is the VHF radio and it's transmitted over a certain frequency and there's a receptor that takes a relay and it receives all of these reports in real-time, and then transmits them to the person who is to receive these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With respect to the soldiers that entered one of the hospitals, do you know, were those individual soldiers? Was it a platoon? Was it a larger unit of soldiers? How many soldiers went into the hospital, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that based on what I heard is that there was a platoon that was there and they told us that there were soldiers that had penetrated the hospital and they were opening fire from the hospital. Apart from that, I can't give you more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said there was a platoon that was there. Are you referring to the CANBAT platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We had the equivalent of some 30 persons who were to handle the management of the hospital. I cannot give you the names of the soldiers of the HVO who were using the hospital or who were members of the company or the platoon or the battalion that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that any patients were injured in any fighting in or around the hospital on the occasion that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, fortunately not. When the situation took place, we moved the patients to upper levels in the hospital, and so their peace of mind enabled them to move them out of harm's way. Indeed when we look at the injuries that people may have received there or may have come from some of the fire coming from the BiH troops and returning fire to the HVO troops, but fortunately our soldiers did move the patients to avoid any harm coming to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that there were allegations that chemical weapons had been used in the course of the conflict in November, 1993 in and around Fojnica. What side was it alleged to that conflict had used chemical weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to repeat, it was the BiH that indicated that the HVO had used them. Our own investigation did not enable us to confirm that, and the Canadian battalion found that there was no use of any type of weapons of this type. I did not carry this any further because the investigation did not enable us to divulge this. We were using a special kind of camera which would enable us to detect the presence of these type of products in the air and we used these products, we found nothing at all. And so there was no proof whatsoever that any chemical agents had been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have described allegations that patients were directed into mine fields in order to discover the presence of mines. Was this related to you by other members of CANBAT as activities they had seen or activities that were related to them by the mental patients or psychiatric patients; if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we come back now, I want to talk to you about the responsibility in that area. It was said that this did, indeed, take place, but I don't know whether or not these activities were reported by patients to CANBAT or whether or not this was seen. But I know that in one particular ^^ corps, it was our soldiers who were witnesses to this event, where one elderly patient was brought by the soldiers, the Croatian-- or, rather, the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in one particular 'corps' it was our soldiers who witnessed the event. What do you mean by corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There must be an error in translation. What I said that in one particular case, in one particular case, this was not a report, if you will, of a report. This was one of our own members of our own Canadian battalion that was a witness to that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This was a sending of a patient into a mine field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the patient Muslim, Croat; do you know, or was it not reported to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it didn't have any importance to us and I don't remember the ethnic background of the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The convoys that you've described coming under fire on the way to the hospitals in Bakovici and Drin, I believe was the town, were those UNHCR convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I explained, we don't have that particular document, but the road, when we would go to the west from Kiseljak, from Kiseljak to Busovaca, that would then go towards the north-west. For Fojnica, it would go towards the west and curve and then go to the Southwest. Now, the first part of that road was under the control of the HVO. After that you went into what I referred to as a no-man's land. And this particular area was always under fire and, for this reason, we recommended very strongly to the UNHCR not to use any trucks or any civilian vehicles; rather, in this area, because of the imminent danger of being attacked, and so we used our own vehicles, military vehicles for this. Each time we have any type of convoy, we had to have some sort of written authorisation because it was to make sure these were humanitarian aid being transferred, but in military vehicles. So the forces there from the HVO knew very well what was contained in this convoy and what type of goods were being transported in these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could retrieve the easel for a few questions I have in mind. I have some other questions to ask you in the mean time. You said that, to your knowledge, there was no BiH army presence in the Kiseljak enclave. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was no BiH units working or active within the Kiseljak enclave, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What time or times do you have in mind when you give that testimony, the entire period of both of your tours or something less than that point -- those points in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as from the time period in which I arrived in spring, 1993 and also during my other tour of duty in October, 1993 to May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So during both of your tours, that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the Territorial Defence is or TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there TO units in the Kiseljak enclave during either of your tour of duties -- tours of duty, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there were no units organised for Territorial Defence. If we can say that there were some men of Muslim origin who were still living in the Kiseljak enclave, as I stated, it was not rare, it was quite frequent for these men to possess hunting weapons, personally weapons and it's quite probable that if an attack had been launched against the village, that these men would protect their own families. If they are saying now that these men, as a group, would constitute some sort of unit that was responding to a command of the BiH, well then, there I would not agree with that line of thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Defence Exhibit 125 could be placed before the witness, Mr. President, and on the ELMO. Recognising that this document, Captain, is in the BSC language, I'm going to tell you that this document purports to be an organisational schemata of Territorial Defence or TO units in certain locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including in the Kiseljak municipality. I'm going to ask my colleague to read the names of the locations underneath the Kiseljak box, if you will, which is in the lower centre portion of the diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The title of the whole document is the Municipal Staff of the Armed Forces and it shows the units of the municipal staff of the armed forces of Kiseljak belonging to that headquarters. If we read the central portion, we have the Kiseljak unit, then the 4th of July, then the Rotilj, then the Palez unit, and the Palez Trebinje unit. To the right we have Topole, Radanovici, Han Ploca, Ljubinje, and Bakovici, and to the left, Gromiluk, Brestovsko and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it, Captain, that you would be surprised to learn that there were TO units in these locations in 1992 and '93 up to the conflict that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm objecting to this point. I really strongly object. This is a document that has not been admitted into evidence. The witness yesterday didn't recognise it. This witness has never seen it. There's no date on it, it can't be placed in time. It is absolutely absurd to ask this witness about whether he knows anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What's important, Mr. President, is if he doesn't, that be in the record, because if ultimately in this case this document is proven to be authentic and to represent facts at relevant periods in time, then that's information the court should have. This is not information he has and he doesn't factor any such information into the opinions that he's given the court. That's my purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges' opinion yesterday was to say, and I think they will continue to maintain that rule, that first of all the documents should be admitted or not, that the discussion should first take place and not constantly talking about a document which will not be admitted. The Registrar has just said that this document was admitted, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My understanding from my colleague, Mr. Harmon, was that it was not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As regards the document D125, yesterday it was said that the witness did not recognise the document because he had never seen it. However, the stamp was the same as on D124 and, for that reason, the Trial Chamber admitted D125. In any case, this had to do with -- this was valid for yesterday's witness and I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, I can ask the witness whether this is a document which you can identify either through the stamp or through the data or other contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not ever seen this document as such. I don't see the date. I do recognise the symbol in the middle of the stamp, but during the time that I was there, I didn't ever see a stamp which indicated a BiH army stamp with Kiseljak on it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So I don't recognise this document. Therefore, this document is not -- you don't recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. It is not recognised and it cannot be admitted. No point in going on or talking any more about a document which isn't not admitted, however, your comments have been indicated in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you may?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I believe, since I spoke to most of the civilian authorities and military authorities on the ground, when they talk about Bilalovac and Kacuni, and I do think that the authorities in place would have spoken to me about this had they known about it. I wasn't aware -- as far as I know, there were no organised units for the reasons that I say. That is, when I spoke to the municipal authorities of those places, I was never told that the Territorial Defence forces existed and I think that they would have told me that, given my relations with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with this comment, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to thank you for permitting the witness to put an answer into the record. And thank you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please move on to another question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You've described the chain of command of the HVO as you perceived it. Do you know, was one of the purposes of the Busovaca joint commission so that commanders could go into the field to try and persuade local soldiers to obey the cease-fire that had been ordered by Colonel Blaskic and General Haji Hasanovic of the third corps, was that one of the purposes of the Busovaca joint commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember if it was one of the specific points or purposes of the commission at the time. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree with the following characterisation? Suddenly, a very large column of dispirited Croat soldiers appeared in Vitez. They were not soldiers at all, very few had had any real training. They could handle their weapons all right, but were really civilians in uniform. I'm reading from Colonel Stewart, Broken Lives, page 92. Do you agree with that characterisation of some or all HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have the pleasure of reading Colonel Stewart's book. This is an excerpt taken out of context. What period are you talking about? It's hard for me to qualify something or to say anything about it, unless I know that. What I can say is that I didn't operate in Vitez. I went through Vitez several times in order to go to the British battalion or the headquarters in there, but that was not part of my zone of responsibility, so I don't think I can really add to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Move to another question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that Vinko Lucic was the liaison officer in Kiseljak posted by the HVO central command in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in that capacity that he introduced himself to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you understood that to mean that he reported directly to the HVO command in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is common practise when a liaison officer moves first from top to bottom and then from right to left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that during the period of time you were having contacts with Vinko Lucic, you were not having contacts with liaison officer that reported to the operational zone for central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no contact because I was told that my contact point would be Vinko Lucic, only he. I can't tell you why I was restricted in that way. This is an observation that I had to accept. Lucic was not a commander, he was a liaison officer, and I would not be in a good position to tell you why he was put in that place. It was never clear in my mind. It was never clear why I had to work with Lucic, rather than with the commander who was responsible for the zone in which the Canadian battalion was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You've described using a dirt road between Vitez and Kiseljak. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you said you used it once. Can you tell us with as much specificity as you can, when did you use this road? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, it must be the very end of April or beginning of May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, looking at the map, and there are two maps, one on top of each other, one is of the Vitez/Busovaca area, the other is in the Kiseljak area. If you would like to look at it to answer this question, please feel free. But my first question is: You said the road left Vitez to the south and then to the south-east. Did this road go through Krujitsa? If you would like to look and see where Krujitsa is, feel free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I prepared myself for coming here, I tried to find the road. As I was explaining, the topographical maps I had were photocopies, but I remember approximately the road that went from south of Vitez, it went first to the south and then it would cut out to the south-east. I cannot tell you. I tried to find the map and to see the map, but I can't really give you a specific answer. If you have an aerial view, then I think that we would be able to retrace the road on an aerial photo, but when I see it on the map, I guess I could not -- I couldn't draw the road for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're saying you cannot draw it on a topographical road, such as the JNA Zenica 4 map which has been produced and put on the easel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. As I said in my testimony this morning, I knew that -- I had been told there was a road. I almost found it by chance in the field at an intersection of two roads. I was still travelling around blindly because I couldn't find my way around on the map. So I really cannot draw it for you on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We'll go on to some other questions and I'm going to ask my co-counsel to get an overhead transparency and get the Registrar's assistance in locating an aerial photograph, I know there's several in evidence, at least of the Vitez area, so the witness can draw at least the beginning of this road so we can determine this origin. So as not to hold up proceedings, I have other questions, just a few more, not very many. I'll continue with those and perhaps we can find that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I just want to ask for confirmation of Captain Lanthier. Would you, perhaps, be able to find the road with an aerial photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, if I saw an aerial photograph from -- showing Vitez to the Kiseljak enclave, I may be able to find a road which goes from one point to another. That's what I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hayman, please continue with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If Mr. Nobilo could be excused for the moment to retrieve the necessary supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any occasion, can you tell us of any occasion during either of your tours when an HVO personnel used this dirt road or path?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no personally knowledge because I didn't go with anybody from the HVO who used that road, but what I saw or what I noted is simply there was a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether this road passed through territory that was controlled by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we alluded to this earlier. There would be BiH forces surrounding the enclaves. What I think is important to point out here is they were not defensive positions, that is, that there was not a line of obstacles and trenches all along the perimeter, so it's possible that under good conditions that one could travel from one point to another, even if one had to go through some of the territory that the other side was controlling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described the level of cooperation from the BiH army compared to the HVO. Were any circumstances -- did any circumstances arise during either of your tours where it was necessary for CANBAT to use lethal force against any combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question, whether we were called on to deploy the Canadian elements against one of the three warring factions? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question was, did circumstances arise during either of your tours when CANBAT were called upon to fire upon BiH army, or Croat, HVO persons, to fire on any of the warring parties as an act of defence or whatever? Did that become necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Canadian battalion on several occasions did fire against the three warring parties. At some point we even conducted a blocking operation in the exclusion zone of Sarajevo. So, yes, we did respond for our own self-protection by firing on the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You gave an opinion that the HVO engaged in systematic ethnic cleansing, which fact was demonstrated by the Stupni Do massacre. Let me ask you if you've ever received the following information and, if you hadn't, if receiving it would change that opinion, and I'm going to read a passage from an ECMM daily summary dated the 2nd of November, 1993. I can provide a copy to counsel so they can read along, if they wish, and I will make -- I do think a copy should be put into the record. In paragraph 1, it states: "HCC, which I believe is the reference to one of the ECMM centres in the area, met with ‘blank', and I'll leave the name out in case it's something that shouldn't be stated, a member of the BiH operative group in Daravina, who explained after being asked why the Stupni Do massacre took place. Stupni Do was the local gateway to BSA (Bosnia-Serb Army) controlled territory which made it a most lucrative centre for smuggling and black marketing. The residents of Stupni Do became reasonably well to do with this arrangement but had to pay a percentage to the HVO. In early October, the HVO demanded a substantially higher cut and were told no by Stupni Do authorities. As a result of this answer, HVO authorities in Kiseljak, Vares and Kakanj coordinated the activities that followed. Those who were killed in Stupni Do were executed deliberately for their part in the black market. HVO trucks then removed black market loot and everything of value to Vares. Comment, ECMM has previously reported on black market activities around Stupni Do. All or part of the above may or may not be true, but all of it is plausible." Captain, have you ever received information such as that which I read in the course of your second tour in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from a -- I was in no way involved in the Stupni Do investigation. I know there was a detailed investigation made, but what I can tell you, which does not correspond to what I know about Stupni Do, I stated in my testimony this morning that at the end of April, 1993, the 350th brigade commander -- 304th, rather, brigade commander had said that he was afraid that a similar situation to the one which had taken place in Kiseljak and Vitez would take place as well in Vares. At that point he had indicated to me that Vitez -- that it was the gateway, to an operational zone. I'm talking about the end of 1993, but that this brigade did say, I don't know that there was a base plate. That's the bottom that you put the mortar on to stabilise it, and that was threatened in Stupni Do. And when I went to see the village of Stupni Do, in fact, I did find that base plate which was in territory under HVO control and which was part of mortar and corresponded to the attack on the village of Stupni Do. It's at that point -- May, June, July, August, September. So, this is six months before the Stupni Do massacre had occurred that there were certain indications that it might happen. It's difficult to reconcile all of this. What raises questions in my mind, at least which makes me sceptical, is that I don't know who wrote this document that you're referring to. There was an investigation -- what I was referring to was a report of one individual and not to a systematic report of professional investigators. Is this a perception or something like this? I really can't tell you. I can give you my opinion -- I can't really give you an opinion, rather, about this document that you're showing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions, Mr. President, and then I would like to see if we have an overhead map that is suitable. You described the UN mandate with respect to the UNHCR. Was the UN mandate to keep and maintain the safety and security of the vital road links in the area of responsibility, including 500 metres on either side of those main vital road links; is that a fair statement of the UN mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have the statement of the mission but, in general, it was to support UNHCR in its operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. There was no definite instruction given to do this or that in relation to this or that condition, in relation to what UNPROFOR was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. May I inquire of the Registrar if any overheads were found during the interlude?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think that we have what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Captain, why don't you - if you would be so kind - stand up, take a look at this overhead map and make a determination whether you're going to be able to show us at least the beginning of the road as it left Vitez. While you're doing that, we will try and place an overhead transparency on it, if you are going to be able to show us where the road emanated from in the Vitez area. There's no microphone next to you, so if when you're ready to tell us, I think that we need you to return to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, is there no microphone there?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, there's no microphone available for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Captain has to stand a bit to the side otherwise the Judges can't see anything. I'll ask the Captain to step to the side not too far from his microphone and to make sure the camera is directed on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I also look at the topographic maps that correspond to the region?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Defence will give them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the Registrar could tell us the number of this exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit's 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you would like to go over there as well, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I will wait, Mr. President, until Captain Lanthier has actually -- if he's able to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has the exhibit identified by the Registrar, as well as a topographical map, an exact version of which is already in evidence as a Defence Exhibit entitled Zenica 4, it's a JNA topographical map, 1 to 50,000 scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, take your time. It isn't an easy exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While the Captain is having a look, I would ask that the ECMM I read from simply be marked. I'm not offering it as an exhibit, but I think it should be marked and I would like to offer the Prosecution a copy of it, in all fairness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D134.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I couldn't identify which of these roads is the one. There were several roads. There's one that goes from north to south. I tried to make some comparisons to know which of the roads I might have taken but, I'm sorry, I don't know and I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Hayman, this is the only answer that you're going to get about that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I accept it and I've concluded, Mr. President. Thank you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to turn to Mr. Cayley. Perhaps you have a few additional questions you would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just a few, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Captain Lanthier, my learned friend, Mr. Hayman, asked you a number of questions about these enclaves of Kiseljak and Vares and Vitez. Now, I don't want an opinion, just simply a fact. Was it possible to travel from the enclave of Kiseljak to the enclave of Vares without actually going through Bosnian government held territory? Was it possible for the HVO to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We can't really show here where the confrontation lines were, but Vares and Kiseljak were on the east side and had contacts with the Bosnian Serb army and the movement between the two enclaves was easy. It went through the Bosnia and Serb controlled territory. In fact, they were subjected to the BiH offensive in the fall of 93, and at that time, there was a massive displacement of the Vares population through Kiseljak, through those lines that were under the control by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And not including the road, which you say you took between Kiseljak and Vitez, was it possible to travel between the Kiseljak and Vitez enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want it to be clear that the questions you're asking have to be in relation to the cross-examination. You know that this issue of communication is one which has come back almost from the very beginning of the Blaskic trial. Therefore, if you launch this question again and do not respect the scope of the cross-examination, I will have to give the floor back to the Defence because this is a very sensitive question, as you know, and you have to be very careful that you are remaining within the scope of the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is a linked question. A number of questions were asked about it. I don't intend going through the whole matter again, but I simply want to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than the road link that my learned friend was having you attempt to identify, was it possible to travel between the Kiseljak and Vitez pockets, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question was already asked, Mr. Cayley. Captain, could you give us back your answer again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I know about one of the roads, but if you're asking for an opinion from somebody that was in the field and things, it was not impossible, as an individual, or as a small group to go from one place to another. I'm not referring now to any specific faction, but one could go from one to the other because the terrain was not 100 percent controlled by one or other parties. Under good conditions, one could go, and in the dark one could go from one area to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving on to another area, and I've almost finished, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Referring to the meeting that you had with Colonel Blaskic in Vitez, did Colonel Blaskic make it absolutely clear to you at that meeting that he was in command of the HVO forces within the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear, according to what was said to me. He said he was, indeed, the superior commander of the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did anybody in the HVO ever tell you anything to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear any reports or any personally statements to me that say anything else, other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Captain, you will now receive some questions from the Judges. I will now begin with Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Captain Lanthier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your testimony was clear and very detailed. I would like, nonetheless, to ask you a few questions to have a better idea about certain issues which cover parts of your testimony. My first point is, you stated categorically that General Blaskic had the last word as far as military matters were concerned. You said this. What do you mean by military matters? What type of operations does this include? Does this include, for example, ethnic cleansing? What areas, for example, could this cover of ethnic cleansing in principle? Or would you say this covers only the means by which one arrives at ethnic cleansing? Do you understand what I mean, the military means by which to arrive at ethnic cleansing or simply the ethnic cleansing itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understood it was the use of force that would then lead to ethnic cleansing, so all of the means used in order to arrive at ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It means the execution of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So to exterminate the population or to chase them away or transport them by bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not necessarily putting together the actual plan of the ethnic cleansing, but actually the actual carrying out of the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The principle is at political levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So in the actual execution then of ethnic cleansing, where does the responsibility stop? For example, as you stated there were some of the mentally handicapped who were sent into the mine fields in order to uncover the mines, and also other actions, as you stated, going from house to house in order to burn or to plunder or to kill or to rape. Where is the level of responsibility here? Is it in the main command? You talked about the superior command a moment ago, or was it among the subordinates? Where does the responsibility lay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The responsibility lies with the chain of command. It starts with the commander who gave the order that such an operation be carried out. It also starts with the commander who says such an operation was carried out who, if an action was carried out without his orders, does not take any measures either to court marshal the individuals to carried that out, so the responsibility truly starts with the person who made the initial decision all the way down to the person who carried out the act.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about actions carried out in a secondary -- let's say a secondary area, like in a village. You who know the area, was it difficult for the high command to know about what's going on in such an area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eventually, I think it's impossible for someone not to know what happened, so he must be held responsible for his actions. So if a soldier commits a crime, then it is up to the commander to say, yes, of course, the person is responsible, because you can never be disassociated from now responsibilities. But if these actions are carried out again and again, then the commander becomes responsible because he never imposed his command and made his command felt by the ranks. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand that you also submitted complaints to the authorities. Were these complaints considered? Were you informed of any steps that were taken, or any punishment that was carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never received any report that would indicate when any actions were taken. When I submitted these complaints, I received excuses saying that this was outside of their control and these were, I believe, an attempt felt to escape their responsibility, which was part of the command, which goes with anyone who has a position of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, you stated that Mr. Bradara, you said you spoke with him and you said there were isolated acts -- whether he told you these were isolated acts carried out by frustrated civilians, and you admitted that possibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The other possibility then, was that these were actions carried out by individual soldiers and this you seem to also be excluding as a possibility because this is organised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking about a group of soldiers belonging to a -- if it is a group of soldiers -- I'm sorry. There is some problem with the sound. I'm sorry. To rephrase what I was saying earlier, if this was a group of soldiers which belonged to an organised unit which committed these crimes, then the chain of command becomes responsible, especially if these things are repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you're also excluding the fact that these may be drunken soldiers or, for example, the case of this woman who was raped and then killed and other elderly men were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, we're not talking about an isolated village, we're talking about all of the Kiseljak pocket, something that was orchestrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Orchestrated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I also wanted to ask you a question regarding the sophisticated weapons that were found. You said that there were some missile launchers. You also mentioned that there were some of these caterpillar run vehicles. Did you consider, perhaps, that these might be technically advanced weapons that would be difficult for those parties to obtain; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The point I was trying to make is that logistically speaking, these arms are here. It's quite difficult for these arms to have been here because they had to have been brought through the entire territory, so they must have been held by one or the other of the factions. But to use a weapon such as a missile or a missile launcher of that type, and when the technical situation does not allow it, that means this kind of weaponry must be very readily available. What that tells me also is that the logistical means, whether the line for providing the logistical means must be open. This also gave me the impression, since in the Kiseljak pocket there were no industries available to produce such weapons, that these must have been coming from the outside. These were weapons that are normally made available to a division. I'm talking about my own experience, that the missile launcher is only held at the discretion of the commander. So a battalion or a brigade normally doesn't have this. These are sophisticated weapons which were held at the highest ranks within the command. I'm not saying this is necessarily the case there, but I'm saying that you were to simply look at the presence of these types of weapons, it means that were being obtained elsewhere, outside of the Kiseljak pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you saying from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Another detail, you said in Rotilj, that the women and the children were kept in detention. Why were they detained? Why keep them in detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer that was given to me was that it was for their well-being in order to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that the men were also detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see any of these men, except for my very, very first visit to Rotilj when I saw a man who was working, but the other men I didn't see. I was told they were brought during the day to work in the trenches. Why were they being guarded?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: First of all, where did these inhabitants come from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We must first of all say they come from the Kiseljak pocket or they're persons of Muslim origin, and perhaps this is the process of ethnic cleansing where they cleanse the entire pocket and then they bring all these people to that area. Or perhaps they are bringing people there to carry out an exchange of prisoners, if there are other prisoners, prisoners of war let's say, or other types of prisoners, all these people were being used as a means for negotiations. I'll free such and such a person when such and such a hostage is brought forward. So, if you will, this is a means of negotiation. So I have two reasons in my mind why these people were being detained. One, either for process of ethnic cleansing, or another idea that comes to mind is a bargaining chip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Captain, you spoke at one stage of civilians in uniform, so I take it, of course, you're familiar with the distinction between a career military officer and a civilian in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite honestly, Your Honour, I don't remember when I might have said that there were civilians wearing uniforms. I don't know when I may have said that during my testimony. Besides, when you see an individual in the uniform--.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps you're speaking very quickly. But I think indeed at one point you did talk about uniforms, or perhaps it was from the passage read by Mr. Hayman in which that reference was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really recall. I don't recall having said that, but in the case...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not terribly important whether you said so or not. Are you familiar with the distinction that there might be times when a politician who is essentially a civilian may don a military uniform, although he is not a career military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a distinction that could be made. From looking at someone, I cannot tell whether or not they are a professional soldier or some other type of soldier. The uniform or camouflage uniforms were widespread. People would wear them, not necessarily professional soldiers or members from units or a particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to Mr. Kordic. Did you, in fact, meet with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally met him on two or three occasions. My interaction with Mr. Kordic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think you described him as having political authority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he presented to me the representative -- it was the ECMM representative who presented him to me and he described the persons who were present in the assembly and he described Mr. Kordic as one of the political heads of the HVO. He did not introduce himself to me as such, but he was presented to me in that way, in an indirect way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he in HVO uniform or any uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that, indeed, yes, he was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an impression at the time as to whether he was a career military officer or a civilian in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impression that I had, although I don't know what his president's background is, that I had the a feeling he was a civilian wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk a little bit about Stupni Do. There were certain occurrences there, and after they took place you visited and you saw the condition of the place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stupni Do, I visited for the first time at the end of April, 1993, so before the events of 1993, but in the event that took place in 1993, I visited very briefly after that took place, but I had no part in the investigation that took place there, but I do recall some of the destruction of Stupni Do, but I did not actively take part in the investigation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me put you perfectly at ease. I wasn't suggesting that you took part in the investigations. Now, from what you saw of the condition of the place after certain occurrences happened, are you in a position to help this Trial Chamber by saying whether or not the conditions which you saw were more consistent with the phenomenon of ethnic cleansing or whether they were more consistent with commercially motivated executions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impression I had, Your Honour, is that this was an operation conducted in the same manner as was done in Kiseljak and Vitez, generally speaking, so this was a case of ethnic cleansing. This is my personally opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one last area of interest I have is one about which you have, indeed, spoken more than once. You spoke with Colonel Blaskic and you saw in operation on the ground the military organisation of which he was in charge. Now, from your conversation with him and from what you saw on the ground of his military organisation in operation, are you able to tell the Tribunal whether there were any armed units on the Croatian side who were entirely outside of his authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any evidence that would suggest that there were independent groups operating in that manner. During my conversation I had initially with Colonel Blaskic in mid-March 1993, he did not mention that such organisations may have existed. There are two ways to look at the situation: One could be a case of pride, a commander might hesitate to state that there were organisations operating outside of his command. That could be one of the reasons. Another is that there did not exist any and my impression is that there were none, any type of organisations outside the chain of command operating independently, if you will. ^^ JUDGE RIAD: I am obliged to you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, you've answered a large number of questions in a very clear manner. I would like to have a number of clarifications. How many kilometres are there between Kiseljak and Vitez, using the normal road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say some 30, but you have to measure it to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned this path which did not seem very easy to be used for convoys, nonetheless, you stated you used it with your own vehicle. Does it then seem plausible to you that Colonel Blaskic could have used this particular road quite quickly, given the fact that he is the head of his staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can say that this route was not good for a convoy. We're not really talking about a road but rather a path. It would have taken me a good hour and a half to use -- it took me an hour and a half to use this road. It's a very, very difficult road to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Might I call it an animal's path, it's very small. But would you say, nonetheless, then the inevitable responsibility of Colonel Blaskic would mean that he would be able to move along this path; would you, as a professional career soldier, find it reasonable that the head of staff in the midst of a military situation would waste his time using a path if he felt that this path was not practicable? Or would you feel that would be possible, but not probable, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think it was possible. There were several means of communication, but at a moment in time, the commander must impose his command through physical presence. He can't continually impose his command from a distance and so a commander must be able to make his command known to his troops, so this requires -- if it requires an hour and a half trip, then I find that is quite plausible that Colonel Blaskic would use such a path.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And your general impression, then, is that he was then present in these two locations on an equal level or he was aware of both locations? And now five years later, having reflected on this, you feel that it's all together possible and that you don't have the impression that he simply abandoned Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that he abandoned Kiseljak. I never saw Colonel Blaskic myself in Kiseljak, I never met him there, but this type of -- the path that existed and the responsibilities and the need for a command to be able to be in charge of his divisions, depending on the standards for the military, it would mean that he would not make a trip in without needing to do so. But I thought that if he would need to make such a trip, it was possible to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would it be possible for him to use a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would easily possible to use a helicopter, if such means had been made available. I know that some of the warring factions did, indeed, have helicopters. I saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were told that Colonel -- rather, Mario Bradara informed you of some provisions arriving in the Croatia. Were there any signs of any soldiers, Croatian soldiers -- soldiers from Croatia that were arriving and giving some support to these organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some Croatian soldiers in central Bosnia. I can't tell you whether they came with convoys and I can't make any specific commentary on this, but I can tell you I did see some of these soldiers on the ground. Sometimes we would say that these are soldiers of unknown origin, but I know they were soldiers from Croatia in Bosnia. To say whether they came by that road there, I cannot really say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One last question for you then, with regards to the hospital, the one in Bakovici, or the other one in ^^ Drin. When you say that some of the patients were used in order to detect mines, this is something that's quite horrible. Do you know whether or not the ICRC was ever notified of this? You have a relationship with them. I'm sorry, I was working in English. Do you know what the acronym is in English, is this the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the ICRC did intervene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether or not they themselves went to actually intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Captain, the Tribunal would like to thank you. You have answered very well to the questions. I would like to see whether my colleagues have any supplementary questions. Very well. There are no other questions for you. So the Chamber will now adjourn for this evening. It will resume tomorrow morning solely for the morning session at 10.00. There is one question I would like to ask. You know that -- simply a question regarding the organisation -- do you know there are a number of lawyers who come to attend some of these sessions. I'm not trying to have an idea of what's going to happen in the future for the whole length of the trial, but do you know whether any closed sessions are coming up? Will we have a closed session tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We do not, Mr. President. Tomorrow morning we do not have a closed session, we have a protected witness with some protective measures, but not closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We will now stand adjourned. ---Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of May, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
